issue_title: cmd/fix: automate migrations for simple deprecations
requirement: **Requirement: Automated Migration of Simple Deprecated API Usages in `cmd/fix`**  The `cmd/fix` tool shall automatically rewrite source code that uses deprecated APIs to their recommended replacements when the deprecation is simple and mechanically translatable.  1. **Scope.** The tool shall handle deprecations where the replacement is a direct, semantically equivalent substitution, including renamed functions, renamed identifiers, changed package paths, and calls whose arguments map one-to-one to a new signature. It shall not attempt rewrites that require changing control flow, altering semantics, or making design decisions.  2. **Detection.** The tool shall identify deprecated usages by recognizing the standard `Deprecated:` doc-comment convention and any supported machine-readable migration annotations, and shall resolve references through type information so that only uses of the actual deprecated symbol are rewritten.  3. **Transformation.** For each supported deprecation, the tool shall rewrite the usage to the replacement named in the deprecation, preserving the surrounding code's formatting, comments, and build constraints.  4. **Safety.** The tool shall not modify code when the replacement is ambiguous, when the deprecated symbol has no defined replacement, or when the rewrite would produce code that fails to type-check. In these cases it shall report the location and reason without changing the file.  5. **Output modes.** The tool shall support a dry-run mode that prints proposed changes as a diff without writing files, and an apply mode that writes changes in place.  6. **Imports.** When a rewrite requires adding or removing an import, the tool shall update the import block accordingly and remove imports that become unused.  7. **Verification.** The tool shall be covered by tests that run against golden input and output files for each supported deprecation pattern, including negative cases where no rewrite must occur.  8. **Documentation.** The tool's help output and documentation shall list the classes of deprecations it can automatically migrate and describe how maintainers can mark a deprecation as automatically migratable.

issue_title: cmd/compile: implement powerpc 32-bit backend (ppc32)

issue_title: Make `pub` in a binary equivalent to `pub(crate)` for diagnostics

issue_title: [RFC] TorchStore - A Shared-Memory Tensor Store
requirement: **Requirement: TorchStore – Shared-Memory Tensor Store**  The system shall provide a shared-memory tensor store, referred to as TorchStore, that allows multiple processes on the same host to store, retrieve, and share PyTorch tensors without redundant serialization or copying.  **Functional Requirements**  1. **Put/Get Operations:** The store shall support storing a tensor under a unique key and retrieving it by that key from any participating process on the same machine. 2. **Zero-Copy Sharing:** Tensors stored in TorchStore shall be backed by shared memory so that readers map the same physical memory rather than receiving a copy. 3. **Metadata Handling:** The store shall preserve tensor metadata, including shape, dtype, stride, and device, and shall reconstruct tensors with identical metadata on retrieval. 4. **Key Management:** The store shall support checking for key existence, deleting keys, and listing stored keys. 5. **Lifecycle Management:** Shared memory segments shall be reference-counted or otherwise tracked so that memory is released when no longer referenced, and cleaned up safely if a process terminates unexpectedly. 6. **Concurrency Safety:** Concurrent reads and writes from multiple processes shall be synchronized so that readers never observe partially written tensors.  **Non-Functional Requirements**  1. **Performance:** Put and get operations for CPU tensors shall avoid serialization overhead and complete in time proportional to metadata handling rather than tensor size. 2. **Portability:** The implementation shall support Linux and macOS at minimum; Windows support is optional. 3. **Scope:** The store is limited to single-host, multi-process communication; cross-node sharing is out of scope. 4. **Error Handling:** Operations on missing keys or invalid arguments shall raise clear, documented exceptions.  **Out of Scope**  - Distributed (multi-node) storage. - Persistence to disk across restarts. - GPU tensor sharing via CUDA IPC (may be considered in a follow-up).

issue_title: Improve the indexability (SEO) of Flutter apps on the web
requirement: **Requirement: Improve search engine indexability (SEO) of Flutter web applications**  **Requirement Statement:** Flutter web applications shall produce crawler-accessible, semantically structured web content that enables search engines to discover, crawl, and index the application's textual content, individual routes, and navigation links, without requiring full client-side JavaScript execution.  **Sub-requirements:**  1. **Crawler-readable text:** All user-visible text rendered by Flutter widgets shall be exposed to search engine crawlers as extractable text (via real DOM text nodes, progressive enhancement, or pre-rendered/server-rendered HTML) that accurately corresponds to the visually rendered UI.  2. **Unique, addressable routes:** Each screen or logical content state shall be reachable via a unique, canonical URL with deep-linking support; a direct request to a route URL (including a cold load by a crawler) shall deliver the content corresponding to that route.  3. **Per-route metadata:** The framework shall support setting and dynamically updating per-route document metadata — including `<title>`, meta description, canonical URL, and Open Graph/Twitter Card tags — synchronized with the application's navigation state.  4. **Semantic HTML and crawlable links:** Rendered output shall use standard semantic HTML elements (e.g., headings, lists, alt text) and represent internal navigation as standard `<a href>` hyperlinks so crawlers can interpret page structure and follow links between screens.  5. **Pre-rendering / server-side rendering support:** The framework shall provide a documented, supported mechanism (or stable integration point) for static pre-rendering or server-side rendering of Flutter web content, ensuring indexable content is present in the initial HTML response.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - With JavaScript execution disabled or restricted, a standard web crawler can extract the primary textual content of each major screen of a Flutter web app, and the extracted content matches the visible UI. - Each major screen resolves at a unique URL and returns the correct `<title>`, meta description, and canonical tags for that route. - Internal navigation links are discoverable and followable by a crawler as standard anchors. - An automated SEO audit (e.g., Lighthouse) of a representative Flutter web application reports no SEO failures attributable to the Flutter rendering layer.

issue_title: Implement a Set primitive to complement Dictionary and Array
requirement: The core library shall provide a first-class `Set` collection primitive alongside the existing `Array` and `Dictionary` primitives. A `Set` shall be an unordered, generic collection containing at most one occurrence of each element, using the platform’s standard equality and hashing semantics to determine membership.  The `Set` API shall support:  - Construction from an array literal or iterable - Membership testing and element count - Element insertion and removal - Iteration independent of insertion order - Value equality and hashing - Union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference, including non-mutating and mutating forms consistent with existing collection APIs - Predicates for subset, superset, and disjointness  The implementation shall follow the typing, mutability, and API conventions of the existing `Array` and `Dictionary` primitives and shall include documentation and tests covering uniqueness, membership, mutation, iteration, and set operations.

Specifically, gopls shall: 1. Display, at each concrete (non-interface) type declaration, an annotation (e.g., CodeLens or equivalent client-supported mechanism) listing the interfaces that the type is statically known to satisfy. 2. Display, at each interface declaration, an annotation listing the concrete types that are statically known to implement the interface, including an indication of the count when the list is long. 3. issue_title: Return index of the first visible item in ListView
requirement: **Requirement: ListView First Visible Item Index API**  The ListView component shall provide a public API that returns the zero-based index of the first item that is currently visible within the ListView's viewport.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. The ListView shall expose a method or property (e.g., `getFirstVisibleItemIndex()`) that, when invoked, returns the index of the topmost item that is at least partially visible in the viewport.  2. The returned index shall be an integer value, where 0 corresponds to the first item in the ListView's data model.  3. The calculation shall account for the ListView's current scroll position, including:    - Content scrolled by user interaction (dragging, scrolling).    - Content scrolled programmatically (e.g., via `scrollTo` methods).    - Content scrolled by keyboard or mouse wheel navigation.  4. An item shall be considered "visible" if any portion of its rendered bounds intersects the ListView's viewport; if the API is intended to return only fully visible items, the component shall instead document and enforce this behavior explicitly.  5. If the ListView is empty or no items are visible (e.g., viewport is collapsed or the list is scrolled past its bounds), the API shall return a defined sentinel value (e.g., `-1`), which shall be documented.  6. The returned index shall always reflect the current item order in the underlying data model, including items added, removed, or reordered since the last render.  **Non-Functional Requirements:**  7. The API shall return the index in O(1) time or better, without requiring iteration over the full item list, by leveraging the ListView's internal layout/scroll offset information.  8. The API shall be consistent with the component's existing public API conventions and be available in all supported platforms/renderers.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - Given a ListView with N items and a scroll position of 0, the API returns 0. - Given the ListView scrolled such that the first k items are fully or partially scrolled out of view, the API returns k. - Given an empty ListView, the API returns -1. - Given the ListView is scrolled to the end, the API returns the index of the first visible item at the bottom of the list.

issue_title: Allow explicitly defining interfaces in GDScript
requirement: **Requirement: Explicit Interface Definition in GDScript**  GDScript shall support explicit declaration of interfaces to formalize contracts between classes, enabling compile-time verification of method implementations and static type checking against interface types.  **Functional Specifications:**  1. **Interface Declaration Syntax**: The language shall provide an `interface` keyword to declare interfaces containing abstract method signatures (including parameter names, types, default values, and return types) and property declarations without implementation bodies or default values.  2. **Interface Implementation**: Classes shall explicitly declare implemented interfaces using an `implements` clause (e.g., `class MyClass extends Node implements IInterface`), requiring the compiler to verify at compile-time that all methods and properties declared in the interface are fully implemented by the class.  3. **Interface Inheritance**: Interfaces shall support inheritance from other interfaces via `extends` (e.g., `interface B extends A`), automatically inheriting all method and property contracts from parent interfaces.  4. **Type System Integration**: Interface names shall be valid type annotations, allowing variables and function parameters to be typed as interfaces; the compiler shall enforce that only instances of classes implementing the interface are assigned to such typed references.  5. **Multiple Implementation**: Classes shall be permitted to implement multiple interfaces simultaneously (e.g., `implements IA, IB, IC`).  6. **Runtime Introspection**: The runtime shall support type checking against interfaces (e.g., `object is IInterface` or equivalent API) to verify at execution time whether an object's class implements a specific interface.  7. **Static and Virtual Methods**: Interfaces shall support declaring both instance method signatures and static method signatures, with implementing classes required to provide corresponding static implementations where specified.  8. **Signal Contracts**: Interfaces shall support declaring signal signatures that implementing classes must define.

issue_title: [Poll] Support DistributedDataParallel (DDP) in PyTorch C++ API (libtorch)
requirement: ## Requirement: Native C++ DistributedDataParallel Support in libtorch  libtorch shall provide a public, documented C++ DistributedDataParallel (DDP) API that enables distributed training of `torch::nn::Module` instances without requiring a Python runtime.  ### Functional requirements  - A C++ `DistributedDataParallel` wrapper shall accept a module, an optional distributed process group, and the local device placement. - During initialization, DDP shall synchronize module parameters and buffers from the designated source rank so that replicas begin training with identical state. - Forward execution shall invoke the wrapped module normally. - Backward execution shall compute local gradients through libtorch autograd and synchronize gradients across the process group using the backend appropriate for the selected device. Gradient synchronization shall default to averaging across participating ranks. - DDP shall support:   - Configurable gradient bucketing and `gradient_as_bucket_view`.   - Detection and handling of unused parameters.   - Optional buffer synchronization before forward execution.   - Static-graph training configurations.   - Gradient accumulation and a scoped mechanism for temporarily disabling gradient synchronization. - The wrapper shall expose module state access, including parameters, buffers, and `state_dict()`, with behavior consistent with Python `torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel`. - The implementation shall work with existing libtorch distributed backends, including Gloo on CPU and NCCL on CUDA when available. - Distributed communication failures and invalid configurations shall be reported as libtorch errors rather than being silently ignored.  ### API and integration requirements  - The API shall follow existing libtorch C++ naming, ownership, device-placement, and exception conventions. - DDP shall interoperate with native C++ optimizers, autograd, and module serialization workflows. - Public headers and reference documentation shall describe construction, forward/backward usage, process-group initialization, cleanup, and backend/device requirements.  ### Acceptance criteria  - Automated tests shall launch training with at least two ranks and verify that replicated parameters remain synchronized, gradients match the expected distributed values, and optimizer updates produce equivalent results across ranks. - Tests shall cover CPU/Gloo execution, CUDA/NCCL execution when enabled, unused parameters, gradient accumulation, disabled synchronization, and buffer synchronization. - A documented C++ example shall demonstrate initializing a process group, wrapping a module, constructing and stepping an optimizer, and running a distributed training iteration.

issue_title: Godot C# GDExtension Roadmap Discussion
requirement: **Requirement: First-Class C# Support for GDExtension Development in Godot**  Godot shall provide a supported workflow for authoring GDExtensions in C# so that developers can build, load, and debug native extensions using C# without writing C++ glue code.  **Functional Requirements**  1. The engine shall load C# GDExtension libraries through the same registration and lifecycle mechanism used for native GDExtensions. 2. The C# binding layer shall expose Godot classes, methods, properties, signals, and enums to C# GDExtension code with type mappings consistent with the existing GDScript and C++ bindings. 3. The toolchain shall generate or provide C# bindings from the Godot API JSON for the engine version in use. 4. Projects shall be able to register custom classes, virtual method overrides, and exported properties from C# GDExtension code, and have them appear in the editor inspector and scene tree. 5. C# GDExtensions shall support hot reload during editor sessions, or document the limitations where hot reload is not supported. 6. The build system shall produce platform-specific artifacts for all officially supported export targets (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, Web where applicable) from a single C# project configuration.  **Non-Functional Requirements**  1. Runtime overhead of C# to engine calls shall not exceed the overhead of the equivalent C++ GDExtension calls by more than a documented margin, measured on a defined benchmark suite. 2. Memory ownership rules for Godot objects passed across the managed/native boundary shall be documented and enforced to prevent leaks and use-after-free errors. 3. Errors crossing the boundary (exceptions, null references, invalid method calls) shall be reported to the editor console with stack traces. 4. The feature shall be covered by automated CI tests on every supported platform.  **Acceptance Criteria**  1. A sample C# GDExtension that defines a custom Node subclass with an exported property and a virtual override runs on all supported desktop platforms. 2. The sample can be exported to at least one mobile or web target without modification beyond the export configuration. 3. Public API documentation and a getting-started guide are published with the release. 4. Roadmap milestones, open design questions, and known limitations are tracked in the issue linked to this requirement.

issue_title: [RFC] PT2-Friendly Traceable, Functional Collective Communication APIs
requirement: # Requirement: PT2-Compatible Functional Collective Communication APIs  ## Summary  Provide functional, traceable collective communication operations for `torch.distributed` that `torch.compile` (TorchDynamo, AOTAutograd, and TorchInductor) can capture, reorder, and optimize without graph breaks, hidden side effects, or loss of correctness.  ## Background  Existing collectives in `torch.distributed` (for example, `all_reduce`, `all_gather_into_tensor`, and `reduce_scatter_tensor`) are in-place and return `Work` handles that must be explicitly waited on. These semantics conflict with the PT2 compiler stack, which requires operations to be pure, schedulable, and expressible in an FX graph.  ## Functional Requirements  1. **Out-of-place semantics.** Each collective must return a new tensor and must not mutate its input tensors or any other tensor argument.  2. **Traceability.** Each collective must be registered as a PyTorch operator in a dedicated namespace (for example, `_c10d_functional`) so that it:    - Is captured as a single node in FX graphs produced by TorchDynamo without graph breaks.    - Has Meta and Fake implementations that compute output shape, dtype, and device without launching communication.  3. **Deferred synchronization.** Collectives must not require the caller to block on a `Work` handle. Synchronization must be expressed through a wait operation (for example, `wait_tensor`) or a tensor subclass (for example, `AsyncCollectiveTensor`) that blocks only when the tensor's data is first accessed. The compiler must be able to move the wait operation within the graph.  4. **Autograd support.** Each functional collective must define a backward formula that is itself a functional collective. For example, the backward of `all_gather` is `reduce_scatter`, and the backward of `all_reduce` is `all_reduce`.  5. **Group identification.** Process groups must be specified in a form that is serializable and traceable, such as a group name plus ranks and tag, rather than an opaque Python object. The group must be resolvable at runtime from within compiled code.  6. **Core operation set.** At minimum, the following must be provided: `all_reduce`, `all_gather_into_tensor`, `reduce_scatter_tensor`, `all_to_all_single`, `broadcast`, and `wait_tensor`.  7. **Eager-mode parity.** Results of functional collectives in eager mode must match the results of the corresponding legacy collectives for the same inputs, including reduction operator, dtype handling, and ordering semantics within a process group.  8. **Compiler scheduling.** The Inductor backend must be able to reorder collectives relative to independent compute and overlap communication with computation, while preserving data dependencies and the ordering required for correctness across ranks.  ## Non-Functional Requirements  - **Backward compatibility.** Existing `torch.distributed` APIs must remain unchanged. Functional variants must be additive. - **Performance.** Under `torch.compile`, functional collectives must not introduce more than negligible overhead compared with legacy collectives, and must enable communication/computation overlap where the legacy path does not. - **Deadlock safety.** Compiled graphs containing collectives must not deadlock when ranks compile or trace differently, and the implementation must document the ordering guarantees that ranks must respect. - **Backends.** The functional API must work with at least the NCCL and Gloo backends.  ## Acceptance Criteria  - A model using functional collectives under `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` compiles with no graph breaks attributable to the collective calls. - Forward and backward results match eager legacy collectives within numerical tolerance for `all_reduce`, `all_gather`, `reduce_scatter`, and `all_to_all`. - Fake-tensor tracing of each functional collective produces correct output metadata without requiring an initialized process group. - Inductor-generated code overlaps at least one collective with independent compute in a representative tensor-parallel or FSDP-style workload. - Unit tests cover eager, compiled, and autograd paths for every operation in the core set on NCCL and Gloo. - Documentation describes the functional API, the wait semantics, and migration from legacy collectives.

issue_title: cmd/compile: implement powerpc 32-bit backend (ppc32)
requirement: # Software Requirement  **ID:** REQ-CMD-COMPILE-PPC32 **Title:** Implement a 32-bit PowerPC (GOARCH=ppc) backend for the Go toolchain **Type:** Feature — New platform support **Primary Component:** `cmd/compile` (with supporting changes in `cmd/link`, `cmd/asm`, `cmd/dist`, `internal/buildcfg`, `go/build`, and `runtime`)  ## 1. Summary The Go toolchain shall support building and running Go programs on 32-bit PowerPC systems via the target `GOARCH=ppc`. The initial supported configuration shall be `GOOS=linux`, `GOARCH=ppc`, big-endian, ELF32.  ## 2. Motivation The toolchain currently supports only 64-bit PowerPC (`ppc64`, `ppc64le`). Go programs cannot be built for 32-bit PowerPC hardware and operating systems still in active use (legacy Linux distributions, embedded/board-level PowerPC, older desktop-class PowerPC machines). This requirement closes that platform gap.  ## 3. Functional Requirements  **FR-1 — GOARCH registration.** The toolchain shall recognize `ppc` as a valid GOARCH value across `cmd/dist`, `internal/buildcfg`, `go/build`, and `go env`/`go tool dist list`. Build constraint evaluation shall report the tags `ppc`, `powerpc`, and `32bit` as true for this configuration, consistent with existing family/word-size tag semantics. Invalid GOOS/GOARCH combinations shall be rejected with clear errors.  **FR-2 — Code generation.** `cmd/compile` and `cmd/internal/obj/ppc` shall generate correct 32-bit PowerPC machine code, including: - 32-bit register model, instruction selection, and SSA rewrite rules for ppc32; - correct decomposition of 64-bit integer operations (multiply, divide, wide shifts, 64-bit compares) into 32-bit instruction sequences; - conformance to the System V ABI for 32-bit PowerPC (argument registers r3–r10, results in r3/r4, stack frame layout and alignment), noting that 32-bit SysV uses direct function pointers, unlike ppc64 ELFv1 function descriptors; - big-endian data layout and ELF32 object emission, including correct DWARF and pclntab metadata for debugging and traceback.  **FR-3 — Linker.** `cmd/link` shall support ELF32 big-endian PowerPC objects for linux/ppc, for internal linking initially, with external linking supported to the extent required by the standard library and cgo staging (see Constraints).  **FR-4 — Runtime.** Package `runtime` shall provide the required ppc32 assembly implementations (goroutine switching, stack growth, deferred calls, GC write barriers, save/restore of g, etc.) and shall apply correct memory layout, pointer size (4 bytes), word alignment, and GC bitmap/heap layout behavior for a 32-bit big-endian target.  **FR-5 — Shared infrastructure.** Common ppc64/ppc code (opcodes, register definitions, utilities) shall be factored or extended so that adding ppc32 causes no regression to ppc64/ppc64le code generation.  **FR-6 — Cross-compilation.** `GOOS=linux GOARCH=ppc go build` shall succeed when cross-compiling from any supported host; native bootstrap on ppc32 is desirable but not required for initial delivery.  ## 4. Acceptance Criteria - **AC-1:** `GOOS=linux GOARCH=ppc go build` produces an executable ELF32 big-endian PowerPC binary that runs correctly on a 32-bit PowerPC Linux environment. - **AC-2:** The standard library compiles for linux/ppc, and `go test std` passes on linux/ppc, excluding only documented platform-specific test exceptions. - **AC-3:** Existing architectures (`ppc64`, `ppc64le`, and all others) build and pass their test suites without regression. - **AC-4:** `go env` and `go tool dist list` correctly report the new configuration.  ## 5. Constraints and Assumptions - Initial scope is limited to `GOOS=linux`, `GOARCH=ppc`, big-endian. - Correctness takes precedence over performance; ppc32-specific scheduling/peephole optimization beyond shared ppc passes is deferred. - Targets without hardware floating point (soft-float) are out of scope for the initial implementation. - cgo support is desirable and may be delivered in a staged follow-up if it would otherwise block core backend delivery.  ## 6. Out of Scope - Additional GOOS values for ppc32 (e.g., aix, freebsd) — to be addressed by follow-up requirements. - Performance parity with ppc64 backends.

issue_title: RFC: Introduce `setup`, `teardown`, and `fixture` attributes for `cargo test`
requirement: **Requirement: Support `setup`, `teardown`, and `fixture` Attributes in `cargo test`**  **Summary:** `cargo test` shall support attributes that let test authors declare setup, teardown, and fixture logic for test functions, so that shared test preparation and cleanup do not have to be duplicated inside each test body.  **Functional Requirements**  1. **Setup attribute:** The system shall allow a function annotated with a `setup` attribute to run before each test to which it applies. The setup function's result shall be available to the test if it returns a value. 2. **Teardown attribute:** The system shall allow a function annotated with a `teardown` attribute to run after each test to which it applies, regardless of whether the test passed, failed, or panicked. 3. **Fixture attribute:** The system shall allow a function annotated with a `fixture` attribute to produce a reusable test resource. Fixtures shall support a declared scope (at minimum per-test and per-test-binary/module) that determines how often the fixture is constructed and destroyed. 4. **Application scope:** The attributes shall be applicable to free functions within a test module and shall apply to all `#[test]` functions in that module, or to specific tests when explicitly referenced. 5. **Ordering:** When multiple setup or teardown functions apply to the same test, they shall execute in a deterministic, documented order. Setup functions shall run in declaration order; teardown functions shall run in reverse order of setup. 6. **Failure handling:**    - If a setup function fails or panics, the associated test shall be reported as failed, the test body shall not run, and any teardown functions whose setup already completed shall still run.    - If a teardown function fails or panics, the failure shall be reported without suppressing the result of the test itself, and remaining teardown functions shall still run. 7. **Parallel execution:** Fixtures with per-test scope shall not be shared between tests running concurrently. Fixtures with broader scope shall be synchronized so that they are constructed at most once per declared scope and are safely accessible from parallel tests. 8. **Test filtering:** Setup, teardown, and fixture functions shall not be executed for tests that are filtered out or skipped via `cargo test` filtering or `#[ignore]`. 9. **Output:** Failures originating in setup, teardown, or fixture code shall be identified distinctly in test output, indicating the phase (setup, test, or teardown) and the originating function name.  **Non-Functional Requirements**  10. **Backward compatibility:** Existing test code without these attributes shall compile and behave identically. 11. **Compile-time validation:** Invalid usage (e.g., a setup function with an incompatible signature, or a fixture referenced but not defined) shall produce a compile-time error with a message identifying the offending item. 12. **Performance:** The overhead added by the attributes to a test with no applicable setup, teardown, or fixtures shall be negligible. 13. **Documentation:** The Rust Book and `cargo test` reference shall document the attributes, their scopes, execution ordering, and failure semantics.  **Acceptance Criteria**  - A test module with one `setup` and one `teardown` function runs setup before and teardown after every test in the module, verified by an integration test. - A teardown runs when the test body panics. - A failing setup marks the test as failed, skips the body, and runs completed teardowns. - A module-scoped fixture is constructed exactly once across all tests in that scope, verified by a counter. - Filtered-out tests do not trigger setup, teardown, or fixture code. - Existing test suites in the Rust ecosystem compile and pass without modification.

issue_title: Add array unpacking/destructuring to GDScript
requirement: ## Requirement: Array Unpacking / Destructuring in GDScript  ### Summary GDScript shall support unpacking (destructuring) of array values into multiple individual variables in a single declaration or assignment statement, so that elements of an array can be bound to separate names without manual indexing.  ### Motivation Today, extracting several elements of an array into distinct variables requires either repeated indexing (`var a = arr[0]; var b = arr[1]`) or per-element accessors. Unpacking makes this concise, readable, and less error-prone, and matches idioms available in other mainstream languages.  ### Functional Requirements  **FR1 — Declaration-time unpacking** A `var` statement that declares multiple variables on the left-hand side and is initialized from an array-like value shall assign each element to the corresponding variable, in order.  ```gdscript var a, b = [1, 2]      # a == 1, b == 2 var x, y, z = [1, 2, 3] ```  **FR2 — Explicit destructuring syntax** An optional bracketed form shall be supported for clarity and for forward compatibility with dictionary/struct destructuring:  ```gdscript var [a, b] = [1, 2] ```  Both forms shall be accepted; the bracketed form is the recommended style.  **FR3 — Assignment to existing variables** Unpacking shall also work in a plain assignment to already-declared variables:  ```gdscript var a: int var b: int a, b = [1, 2] ```  **FR4 — Type inference and static typing** - When a variable in an unpacking statement has no explicit type annotation, its type shall be inferred from the corresponding element of the right-hand array. - Explicit type annotations shall be honoured and statically validated against the element type (e.g. `var a: int, b: String = [1, "two"]`). - Untyped arrays shall not cause the unpacked variables to be typed as `Array`.  **FR5 — Source of the array** The right-hand side may be any expression that evaluates to an array, including literals, function return values, member variables, and `Packed*Array` types. Iteration order shall be the array's index order.  **FR6 — Nested unpacking** Unpacking shall support nested arrays to arbitrary depth:  ```gdscript var [a, [b, c]] = [1, [2, 3]] ```  **FR7 — Error handling** The parser/analyzer shall raise a clear compile-time error (or runtime error, where the value is not statically known) for: - The number of variables exceeding the number of elements in the array. - The number of variables being fewer than the number of elements in the array, unless an explicit "rest"/ignore syntax is provided. - Unpacking a value that is not an array or array-like (e.g. an `int`, `String`, or `Dictionary`). - Mismatched types for explicitly typed variables. Error messages shall identify the offending statement, the expected count, and the actual count.  **FR8 — Ignore/rest syntax (optional, follow-up)** A trailing underscore-based placeholder shall be permitted to explicitly discard extra elements, e.g. `var [a, b, _] = [1, 2, 3]`. If this syntax is not implemented in the initial release, the error behavior in FR7 shall apply instead.  **FR9 — Backwards compatibility** Existing GDScript code, including `for` loop destructuring (`for a, b in pairs:`), tuple-like returns via arrays, and single-variable assignments, shall continue to compile and behave identically. No existing valid program may change semantics.  **FR10 — Documentation and tooling** The GDScript documentation (language reference) shall include a section describing unpacking with examples, error conditions, and supported forms. Syntax highlighting, code completion, and the built-in script editor shall not misparse the new syntax.  ### Non-Goals - Destructuring of dictionaries, objects, or structs (may be added later). - Pattern matching. - Changes to `for` loop semantics.  ### Acceptance Criteria 1. `var a, b = [1, 2]` results in `a == 1` and `b == 2`. 2. `var [a, [b, c]] = [1, [2, 3]]` results in `a == 1`, `b == 2`, `c == 3`. 3. `a, b = some_function_returning_array()` correctly binds both values. 4. `var a: int, b: String = [1, "s"]` compiles and produces correctly typed variables. 5. `var a, b, c = [1, 2]` produces a compile-time error with a descriptive message. 6. `var a, b = 5` produces an error stating the value is not an array. 7. All pre-existing GDScript test suite cases continue to pass unchanged.

issue_title: [web] Support compute on separate thread in Flutter Web
requirement: **Requirement: Execute `compute()` Work on a Separate Thread in Flutter Web**  **Problem Statement** On mobile and desktop platforms, Flutter's `compute()` API runs expensive callbacks on a background isolate, keeping the UI responsive. In Flutter Web, isolates are not backed by Web Workers, so `compute()` executes on the main/UI thread, blocking rendering and user interaction during heavy computation.  **Requirement Statement** The Flutter Web engine shall support executing work submitted via `compute()` (and equivalent isolate APIs, e.g., `Isolate.run`) on a separate thread (Web Worker) so that computation does not block the main UI thread.  **Functional Requirements** 1. When a Flutter Web application calls `compute()` with a top-level function and message, the engine shall execute the callback on a background thread (Web Worker) instead of the main UI thread. 2. Arguments passed to `compute()` shall be correctly serialized/transferred to the worker thread, and results shall be correctly returned to the caller on the main thread. 3. Exceptions thrown within the computed callback shall be propagated to the calling code on the main thread, preserving the error message and type to the extent the platform allows. 4. The main UI thread shall remain responsive (rendering, animations, and input handling continue) while a computation is running. 5. When the target environment does not support Web Workers, or when the callback cannot be transferred (e.g., it is not a top-level function or captures unsendable state), the engine shall fall back to executing the work on the main thread and surface this behavior in documentation.  **Constraints / Non-Functional Requirements** - No changes to the application-facing `compute()` API shall be required; existing valid `compute()` calls shall work without modification. - Behavior shall be consistent across all browsers supported by Flutter Web, with graceful degradation where workers are unavailable.  **Acceptance Criteria** - A CPU-intensive task run via `compute()` in Flutter Web does not freeze the UI; animations continue and user input is processed during execution. - The computation result returned to the caller is correct and matches behavior on non-web platforms. - Errors thrown inside the callback surface as catchable exceptions in the calling code. - The fallback-to-main-thread path behaves identically to current behavior when workers cannot be used.

issue_title: Allow release mode builds to run on simulators
requirement: # Requirement: Support Release-Mode Builds on Simulator Destinations  ## 1. Background / Problem  The build system currently validates the requested build configuration against the target destination and rejects (or silently downgrades to Debug) any `release`-mode build when the destination is a simulator. This restriction was originally introduced because release builds were assumed to require distribution code-signing assets (provisioning profiles, distribution certificates, entitlements restricted to App/Ad Hoc).  As a result, developers cannot exercise release-only code paths — optimization, minification/stripping, `NS_ASSUME_NONNULL` / Swift optimization assumptions, `--release` Flutter/Dart AOT behavior, ProGuard/R8 shrinking, release logging suppression, `assert`/`debugPrint` removal, etc. — on simulator targets. Testing release behavior currently requires a physical device.  ## 2. Requirement  The build system SHALL allow a build with the `release` configuration to be compiled, signed, installed, and launched on iOS simulator destinations.  ### 2.1 Functional Requirements  1. **Configuration/Destination Validation**    - Destination resolution SHALL no longer treat `release` + simulator as an invalid or unsupported combination.    - If a release build is requested with no explicit destination, and no physical device is available, the tool SHALL default to a simulator destination rather than erroring out or falling back to Debug.  2. **Code Signing for Simulator Release Builds**    - Release builds targeting simulators SHALL use local/ad-hoc ("Sign to Run Locally") signing.    - The build SHALL NOT require a distribution certificate, an App Store/Ad Hoc provisioning profile, or any App Store Connect–managed signing asset.    - Entitlements that are unavailable or invalid on simulator (e.g., push notification `aps-environment`, App Groups requiring a real team, Keychain access groups requiring a provisioning profile) SHALL be either omitted for simulator builds or replaced with their simulator-safe equivalents, and the build SHALL NOT fail because of them.    - Any credentials/account (`--team`, `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`, etc.) SHALL remain optional for simulator release builds.  3. **Build Semantics**    - The resulting binary SHALL be a genuine release artifact: release optimization flags enabled, debug symbols/symbol maps produced per existing release rules, and debug-only code paths (assertions, debug logging, dev menus, dev-server bundles) excluded exactly as they would be for a device release build.    - Release builds SHALL remain non-installable on devices and SHALL retain the existing "release builds cannot be uploaded to the App Store from a simulator" guard, if such a guard exists.  4. **Distribution Guards**    - Archive/export/upload flows that lead to App Store or TestFlight distribution SHALL continue to require a physical device and SHALL continue to reject simulator destinations with a clear, actionable error message.  ### 2.2 Non-Functional Requirements  - Existing Debug and profile/release-on-device behavior SHALL be unchanged; no regression in build output, signing identities, or artifact naming. - Simulator release builds SHALL be reproducible and deterministic given the same inputs (no dependence on distribution signing assets). - Errors arising from missing/invalid release configuration SHALL surface clear diagnostics naming the offending setting.  ## 3. User Stories / Use Cases  | ID | As a | I want to | So that | |----|------|-----------|---------| | US-1 | Mobile developer | To run `release` configuration builds on a simulator | I can validate release-mode behavior without a physical device | | US-2 | QA engineer | To install and launch a release-configured app on a simulator | I can test performance-sensitive and release-only code paths in CI | | US-3 | Developer with no distribution certificate | To produce a local release build | I am not blocked by App Store signing assets | | US-4 | Release manager | Attempting to distribute a simulator-built release | I receive an explicit error, preventing accidental invalid uploads |  ## 4. Acceptance Criteria  - [ ] `build --configuration release --destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=<device>'` completes successfully and produces a `.app` bundle. - [ ] The same command succeeds on a machine with no distribution certificate and no provisioning profile installed. - [ ] The produced app installs and launches on the simulator without a signing or entitlement error. - [ ] The built binary contains release optimization/compilation flags and excludes debug-only code, matching the semantics of a device release build. - [ ] `build --configuration release` with no destination and no attached device defaults to a simulator destination and succeeds. - [ ] Archive/export-to-App-Store commands still fail fast when only a simulator is available, with a message directing the user to a physical device. - [ ] Existing unit/integration tests covering configuration × destination matrix are updated to include the `release × simulator` case and pass. - [ ] Documentation (README / build-configuration reference) states that release builds are supported on simulators and explains the local-signing behavior and distribution limitation.  ## 5. Out of Scope  - Enabling TestFlight/App Store distribution from simulator artifacts. - Relaxing requirements for physical-device release builds (distribution signing remains mandatory there). - Changes to the release optimization/minification pipeline itself. - Support for new platforms beyond the existing simulator destinations (e.g., tvOS/watchOS simulators) unless already supported for debug builds.  ## 6. Open Questions  - Should simulator release builds be opt-in via an explicit flag (e.g., `--simulator-release`) or enabled by default for release + simulator? - Should simulator release builds support `arm64` simulator slices only, or also `x86_64` on Intel hosts? - Should entitlements such as Push Notifications be stubbed (no-op) or simply omitted for simulator release builds?

issue_title: x/vuln: add support for suppressing vulnerabilities by ID
requirement: **Requirement: Suppress Specified Vulnerabilities by ID**  **Summary:** The `govulncheck` tool shall allow users to exclude specific vulnerabilities from its reported results by their vulnerability IDs (e.g., `GO-2023-1234`, `CVE-2023-12345`).  **Description:** Users need a way to acknowledge and suppress known vulnerabilities that do not apply to their project, have been accepted as risks, or are awaiting an upstream fix, so that scans report only actionable findings.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. The tool shall accept one or more vulnerability IDs to suppress via a command-line flag and/or a configuration file. 2. The tool shall accept vulnerability IDs in the formats used by the Go vulnerability database (`GO-YYYY-NNNN`) and CVE identifiers (`CVE-YYYY-NNNN+`), and shall match a CVE identifier to its corresponding Go vulnerability entries where aliases are available. 3. Suppressed vulnerabilities shall be omitted from the default text, JSON, and SARIF output. 4. The tool shall report the number of suppressed vulnerabilities in its summary output. 5. The tool shall validate each supplied ID and emit a clear error message for malformed IDs. 6. The tool shall emit a warning for any supplied ID that does not correspond to a known vulnerability, without failing the scan. 7. Suppression shall not alter the exit code except that a scan with only suppressed findings shall exit successfully. 8. Users shall be able to optionally attach a justification or comment to each suppressed ID in the configuration file, which is preserved in documentation output. 9. An option shall be provided to display suppressed vulnerabilities in verbose mode for auditing.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - Given a project affected by `GO-2023-1234` and the suppression of that ID, the scan output does not list `GO-2023-1234` and the exit code is 0. - Given a malformed ID (e.g., `GO-23-1`), the tool exits with a nonzero code and an error message identifying the invalid input. - Given a suppressed ID with verbose mode enabled, the output lists the suppressed vulnerability with its justification. - Given a CVE alias of a suppressed Go vulnerability, the corresponding finding is suppressed.  **Out of Scope:** Suppression by module path, package, or symbol; time-limited suppressions with automatic expiry.

issue_title: Rework the Tilemap terrain system to improve its usability
requirement: **REQ-TILEMAP-TERRAIN-USABILITY-001: Usability Rework of the Tilemap Terrain System**  **Summary** Rework the Tilemap terrain system so that users can create, edit, and maintain terrain-based tile layouts with fewer steps, less manual tile selection, and clearer feedback than the current system provides.  **Background** The current terrain system requires users to manually choose individual tiles and transition pieces to achieve correct edges and corners. This slows editing, produces inconsistent results, and makes terrain behavior hard to predict. The rework addresses these issues without removing existing terrain data or breaking existing maps.  **Requirements**  1. **Terrain painting**    1.1 Users shall paint terrain types onto a tilemap by brush or fill, and the system shall automatically select the correct edge, corner, and transition tiles for the painted area.    1.2 Painting over an existing terrain shall recompute the affected neighboring tiles within one edit operation, with no manual refresh required.    1.3 Users shall be able to adjust brush size between 1x1 and at least 8x8 tiles.  2. **Terrain definition**    2.1 Users shall define a terrain set by mapping tile roles (interior, edge, outer corner, inner corner, and transitions to other terrains) through a single configuration view.    2.2 The configuration view shall display a preview of how each tile role renders when used in a sample layout.    2.3 The system shall validate a terrain set and report missing tile roles before the terrain can be used for painting.  3. **Feedback and visibility**    3.1 The editor shall display the active terrain type and its tile roles while painting.    3.2 The editor shall highlight tiles whose terrain assignment is ambiguous or conflicting (for example, two terrains competing for the same cell) and offer a resolution option.  4. **Editing operations**    4.1 Users shall erase terrain without leaving residual edge or corner tiles, and the system shall update neighboring cells accordingly.    4.2 Users shall undo and redo terrain operations, including recomputed neighbor updates, as a single action per stroke.  5. **Compatibility**    5.1 Existing tilemaps and terrain definitions created before this change shall load without modification and render identically.    5.2 Tile data written by the reworked system shall remain readable by the existing file format version, or a migration path shall be documented and automated.  6. **Performance**    6.1 Recomputing terrain for a 256x256 tilemap after a single brush stroke shall complete within 16 ms on reference hardware, so editing remains interactive.  7. **Documentation**    7.1 User documentation shall include a step-by-step guide for defining a terrain set and painting with it, and a reference for each tile role.  **Acceptance Criteria** - A user can define a complete terrain set and paint a closed region with correct borders in under 2 minutes, without manually placing any transition tile. - All existing terrain-related automated tests pass, and new tests cover neighbor recomputation, erase behavior, and undo/redo for terrain strokes. - Loading a pre-change map produces pixel-identical rendering in a regression test suite. - Missing tile roles are reported before painting begins in 100% of validation test cases.  **Out of Scope** - Changes to the rendering pipeline or tile atlas format. - Support for non-rectangular tile grids. - Procedural terrain generation.

issue_title: Expo like tool for flutter
requirement: The system shall provide an integrated, managed development toolchain and platform for Flutter applications—modeled after the Expo ecosystem—that enables end-to-end development without direct configuration of native platform projects. The toolchain shall fulfill the following capabilities:  1. **Managed Workflow & CLI:** Provide a command-line interface (CLI) to scaffold, configure, and serve Flutter projects with automated management of native iOS and Android build environments. 2. **Universal Companion Client:** Provide a pre-built mobile companion client app (available on iOS and Android) that connects to the local development server via QR code or URL to execute and live-reload application code over the local network without requiring Xcode or Android Studio. 3. **Hardware & Services Abstraction SDK:** Provide a curated, pre-integrated suite of Flutter packages abstracting standard native device capabilities (e.g., camera, location, notifications, filesystem, authentication) compatible with the companion client. 4. **Cloud Build Pipeline:** Provide a cloud-based build and packaging service that remotely compiles production binaries (APK, AAB, and IPA) from source code without requiring local platform-specific build tools. 5. **Over-The-Air (OTA) Updates:** Provide a runtime update service enabling dynamic deployment of non-native code and asset patches directly to distributed applications without requiring app store resubmission.

issue_title: database/sql: missing escape functions
requirement: **Requirement: Provide SQL Escape Utilities in `database/sql`**  The `database/sql` package shall provide functions that safely escape SQL values and identifiers for cases where parameterized placeholders cannot be used, such as table names, column names, and dynamically constructed query fragments.  1. **Identifier escaping:** A function shall take an identifier string (e.g., a table or column name) and return it quoted and escaped for the target dialect, doubling any embedded quote characters so the result cannot break out of the identifier. 2. **String literal escaping:** A function shall take a string value and return an escaped literal suitable for direct inclusion in a SQL statement, correctly handling quotes and backslashes as required by the driver's dialect. 3. **Driver-aware behavior:** Escaping shall be dialect-aware, either through an optional interface that drivers implement or by a driver-provided escaper, so that each driver's quoting rules are respected. 4. **Safety:** Escaped output shall be guaranteed not to alter the structure of the surrounding query when inserted into a valid context. Invalid or unsupported input (such as NUL bytes, where the dialect forbids them) shall produce an error rather than silently producing unsafe output. 5. **Documentation:** The documentation shall state that escaping is a fallback for cases where placeholders are unavailable and that parameterized queries are preferred whenever possible.

issue_title: [video_player] Support DRM content
requirement: **Requirement ID:** REQ-VP-DRM-001 **Title:** Digital Rights Management (DRM) Protected Content Playback  **Description:** The video player component shall support secure playback of DRM-protected audio and video content by integrating with industry-standard DRM systems (e.g., Widevine, PlayReady, FairPlay) to enable encrypted media consumption while maintaining content security throughout the playback pipeline.  **Functional Requirements:** - **FR-1:** The system shall detect DRM-protected content (via manifest metadata or codec signaling) and automatically initialize the appropriate DRM subsystem. - **FR-2:** The player shall acquire decryption licenses from designated license servers using secure, authenticated protocols (e.g., EME/EME-compliant license requests, proprietary license protocols). - **FR-3:** The system shall decrypt protected media segments within a Content Decryption Module (CDM) or secure media path, delivering decrypted frames exclusively to the secure video pipeline. - **FR-4:** The player shall support license persistence, renewal, and expiration handling, including offline license storage where platform capabilities permit. - **FR-5:** The system shall expose standardized DRM status events (license acquired, license expired, license denied, unsupported DRM) to the application layer for UI feedback. - **FR-6:** The player shall enforce output protection controls (e.g., HDCP) when playing DRM content on supported hardware.  **Non-Functional Requirements:** - **NFR-1 (Security):** Decryption keys and plaintext media frames shall never be accessible to the application layer, JavaScript context, or general system memory; all cryptographic operations shall occur within a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or hardware-backed secure decoder. - **NFR-2 (Compliance):** Implementation shall comply with CENC (Common Encryption) standards and W3C Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) specifications where applicable. - **NFR-3 (Performance):** DRM-protected playback shall introduce no more than 5% performance overhead compared to unencrypted playback of equivalent quality. - **NFR-4 (Compatibility):** The solution shall support adaptive bitrate streaming protocols (DASH, HLS) with DRM protection across target platforms (web browsers, mobile, OTT devices).  **Acceptance Criteria:** - **AC-1:** Given a Widevine-protected DASH stream with a valid license server URL, when the user initiates playback, the player acquires the license automatically and begins seamless playback without user intervention. - **AC-2:** Given a PlayReady-protected HLS stream, when the license request fails due to invalid credentials, the player displays a user-friendly error message and does not expose raw error details that could compromise security. - **AC-3:** Given DRM content with an expired license, when the user attempts playback, the system attempts automatic license renewal; if renewal fails, playback is blocked with appropriate messaging. - **AC-4:** Given unsupported DRM content (e.g., FairPlay on an unsupported platform), the player detects the incompatibility before playback initiation and displays a clear "unsupported content protection" error. - **AC-5:** Security audit confirms that memory inspection during playback reveals no plaintext video frames, audio samples, or decryption keys accessible outside the secure decoder boundary.  **Dependencies:** - Valid DRM license server endpoints and credentials provided by content owners. - Platform support for EME (Encrypted Media Extensions) in web environments or native DRM SDKs (Widevine CDM, PlayReady SDK) on native platforms. - Hardware support for secure video path/TEE where high-security content (e.g., 4K UHD) is required.  **Constraints:** - The player consumes DRM-protected content only; content encryption and packaging are out of scope. - Support is limited to industry-standard DRM systems; custom or proprietary DRM implementations are excluded. - License server communication must use TLS 1.2 or higher.  **Out of Scope:** - DRM content encryption, packaging, or key management systems. - Watermarking or forensic tracking features. - Support for legacy DRM systems (e.g., Adobe Access, older versions of Marlin).

issue_title: [feature request] Global GPU Flag
requirement: Requirement: Global GPU Flag  The software shall provide a single, global configuration flag that controls whether GPU acceleration is enabled across the entire application. The flag shall be settable through the standard configuration mechanisms (e.g., command-line argument, environment variable, and configuration file), with a defined precedence order among them. When the flag is enabled, all components that support GPU execution shall use the GPU; when disabled, all such components shall run on the CPU. The flag's current state shall be queryable at runtime and reported in diagnostic or log output. If GPU execution is requested but no compatible GPU is available, the software shall fall back to CPU execution and emit a clear warning rather than failing, unless the user has explicitly configured strict GPU mode. The default value shall be documented.

issue_title: Table > TableRow > TableCell colspan
requirement: **Requirement: Support `colspan` on table cells**  The Table component hierarchy (`Table` > `TableRow` > `TableCell`) shall support a `colspan` property on `TableCell`. The property accepts a positive integer, defaults to `1`, and causes the cell to span that many columns in the rendered table.  **Acceptance criteria:**  1. A `TableCell` with `colspan={n}` (where n > 1) renders as a single cell occupying n columns of the parent table's grid. 2. Subsequent cells in the same `TableRow` are positioned after the spanned columns, not within them. 3. Column alignment, borders, and padding remain consistent across rows that contain spanned cells and rows that do not. 4. Rows with differing cell counts due to `colspan` do not break table layout, header alignment, or the rendering of other rows. 5. `colspan` values less than 1 or non-integer values are rejected or normalized to `1`, with a defined behavior documented. 6. A `colspan` value that exceeds the number of columns in the table is clamped to the available columns or handled with a documented fallback, without throwing an error. 7. `colspan` is available on both `TableCell` in body rows and header cells, if the component supports header cells. 8. The feature is documented in the component's API reference with a usage example. 9. Existing tables without `colspan` render identically to their behavior before this change.

issue_title: Subslice search
requirement: ## Requirement: Subslice Search  ### Overview Extend the project's existing search functionality so that a query can be executed against a *subslice* — an arbitrary contiguous range — of the searchable content, rather than always against the entire content. The same matching engine, options, and result types are reused; only the region that is examined is restricted.  ### Motivation Callers frequently need to find occurrences within a bounded region: a single paragraph or section of a document, one chunk/page of a large file, a user-selected span in an editor buffer, or a sub-range of a row/column-oriented data set. Today the search always traverses the whole input, forcing callers to re-implement matching or to scan and then discard out-of-region results, which is both wasteful and error-prone.  ### Functional Requirements 1. **Region specification** — Search entry points (library API, command-line interface, and any interactive search surface) accept an optional range describing the subslice to search, expressed in a single consistent way (e.g. start/end byte offsets, or inclusive start/exclusive end line numbers). 2. **Restricted matching** — Only occurrences that lie entirely within the specified subslice are returned. Occurrences that begin before, end after, or merely overlap the boundary are not reported. 3. **Result addressing** — Returned matches expose positions both relative to the start of the searched subslice and as absolute offsets into the full underlying content, so that callers can map results back to the original buffer without recomputing offsets. 4. **Boundary semantics** — An empty range, an inverted range, or a range that lies completely outside the content yields an empty result set rather than an error or a panic; out-of-bounds range endpoints are clamped to the content bounds and the clamped region is searched. 5. **Option parity** — All existing search options (case sensitivity, regular-expression vs. literal matching, whole-word matching, multiline mode, capture groups, limits/count) behave identically whether the whole content or a subslice is searched. Multiline patterns must not match across the subslice boundary. 6. **Backwards compatibility** — When no range is supplied, behaviour and output are identical to the current implementation. The new capability is strictly additive and does not change existing defaults. 7. **Exposure across front-ends** — The feature is reachable from every interface that currently offers search, with the range provided in the form natural to that interface (e.g. a `--range start:end` / `--lines a:b` style flag on the CLI, and the current selection/region in interactive surfaces).  ### Non-Functional Requirements - Searching a subslice must not require scanning the whole content; cost should be proportional to the size of the searched region plus the size of the query. - The implementation must not duplicate the matching logic; subslice search reuses the existing engine over the requested region. - The new API is documented, including the coordinate conventions and boundary semantics above.  ### Acceptance Criteria - Searching a subslice returns exactly the occurrences that a whole-content search followed by filtering to that region would return. - A match whose span crosses the region boundary is excluded. - A match that starts exactly at the region start, and one that ends exactly at the region end, is included. - Positions in the result can be converted to absolute content offsets using only the region's base offset. - Empty, inverted, and out-of-bounds regions produce empty results without error. - Existing tests continue to pass unchanged; new unit and integration tests cover the criteria above.

issue_title: Return attention weights in nn.Transformer
requirement: **Requirement: Expose Attention Weights from `nn.Transformer` Modules**  **Background:** Users need access to the attention weight matrices computed inside `nn.Transformer` (and its constituent encoder and decoder layers) for interpretability, visualization, debugging, and analysis tasks. Currently these weights are computed internally during the forward pass and discarded, so they cannot be retrieved without modifying library code.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. `nn.Transformer`, `nn.TransformerEncoder`, `nn.TransformerDecoder`, and their layer classes (`nn.TransformerEncoderLayer`, `nn.TransformerDecoderLayer`) shall accept an optional argument (e.g., `need_weights: bool = False`) that, when set to `True`, causes the module to return attention weights alongside its normal output.  2. Attention weights shall be returned for all three attention types where applicable:    - Encoder self-attention    - Decoder self-attention    - Decoder cross-attention (encoder-decoder attention)  3. The returned structure shall be per layer, so that weights can be retrieved for each of the `N` layers in a stack. The format shall be a list (or tuple) of length `N`, where each element contains the attention weights for that layer.  4. The weights shall be returned as tensors of shape `(batch_size, num_heads, target_len, source_len)` by default, with an option (e.g., `average_attn_weights: bool = True`) to average across heads, yielding `(batch_size, target_len, source_len)`, consistent with the existing `nn.MultiheadAttention` interface.  5. The default behavior (`need_weights=False`) shall remain unchanged, returning only the output tensor, to preserve backward compatibility and avoid performance overhead.  6. Attention weights shall respect existing masks (`src_mask`, `tgt_mask`, `memory_mask`, key padding masks). Masked positions shall reflect the masking applied during computation (e.g., zero probability after softmax).  7. The feature shall work with both the standard PyTorch implementation and the fast path (nested tensor / fused kernels). When the fast path cannot return weights, the module shall either fall back to the standard path automatically or raise a clear, documented error.  8. Weights shall be returned with gradient tracking consistent with the forward pass, so they can be used in differentiable analysis (e.g., attention regularization), with an option to detach them.  **Non-Functional Requirements:**  9. Performance overhead when `need_weights=False` shall be zero beyond a negligible conditional check.  10. Documentation shall describe the return signature, shapes, and the interaction with the fast path and masks, and include a usage example.  11. Unit tests shall verify: correct output shapes for each attention type, equivalence of returned weights with a manual softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V computation, correct behavior under masks, and backward compatibility of the default return value.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - Calling `nn.Transformer(...)(src, tgt, need_weights=True)` returns `(output, encoder_attn_weights, decoder_self_attn_weights, cross_attn_weights)` with per-layer lists as specified. - Existing code calling the module without the new argument produces identical outputs and return types as before. - All new and existing tests pass.

issue_title: cmd/go: allow verifying vendored code
requirement: # Requirement: cmd/go — Support Verification of Vendored Code  ## Background / Problem  Since Go 1.11, the go command supports dependency vendoring (`go mod vendor`), which copies the source of all dependencies into a `vendor/` directory and records the module list in `vendor/modules.txt`.  Vendored trees are widely used in enterprise and security-sensitive builds (air-gapped CI, reproducible builds, FIPS/audit environments) and are commonly committed to version control. Today there is **no way to verify the integrity of vendored source code**:  - `go mod verify` only checks modules in the module cache; it is a no-op (or an error) in vendor mode, and it says nothing about `vendor/`. - `vendor/modules.txt` records only module paths, versions, and replacement/“explicit” annotations — no cryptographic hashes. - Consequently, a modified, corrupted, or maliciously altered file inside `vendor/` is silently accepted by `go build`, `go test`, `go list`, and every other go command operating in vendor mode. Because vendored code is not re-downloaded, the checksums in `go.sum` are never consulted for it.  There is therefore no supported workflow for asserting that vendored code is exactly what the upstream module published, and no way to detect supply-chain tampering or accidental local edits of vendored files.  ## Requirement  The go command must provide the ability to **verify vendored code**: prove that the contents of the `vendor/` directory are byte-for-byte consistent with the module content that the go command would otherwise obtain and validate via `go.sum`.  ## Functional Requirements  ### FR1 — Record module hashes during vendoring  `go mod vendor` must record, for every module it vendors, the module's content hash (the same `h1:`-style dirhash value that appears in `go.sum`) in `vendor/modules.txt`, in a stable, machine-parseable format that associates the hash with the module path and version (including replacement targets).  - The recorded hash must be computed over the module zip content exactly as `go mod download`/`go mod verify` compute it, so that the vendored tree and the module cache agree. - The format must remain a valid `modules.txt` for older go commands: unrecognized metadata must be ignored (not treated as an error) by toolchains that predate this feature, so that older Go versions can still build such a tree. - `go mod vendor` must not require network access beyond what it already requires (hashes must come from `go.sum`/the module cache, never be fetched anew at verify time).  ### FR2 — Verify vendored modules  The go command must expose a way to verify vendored code. Concretely, `go mod verify` operating in a module that has a `vendor/` directory and is in vendor mode must:  1. Verify each module listed in `vendor/modules.txt` by recomputing its content hash over the vendored files and comparing it to the hash recorded in `vendor/modules.txt`. 2. Verify that `vendor/modules.txt` is consistent with `go.mod`: the set of vendored module paths and versions (and replacements) must exactly match the build list computed from `go.mod` and `go.sum`; missing, extra, or version-mismatched entries must be reported. 3. Verify that the set of packages present under `vendor/` matches the packages required by the main module's imports (i.e. that the vendor tree is complete), as far as this is determinable without network access.  Verification must be performed **offline**: no module downloads, no proxy or checksum-database lookups.  ### FR3 — Detection of tampering and corruption  For each mismatch, the go command must report:  - the module path and version, - the file(s) whose content differs from the recorded hash (or, if a per-file listing is not available, the module as a whole), - the expected and actual hash values, - a clear indication of the kind of failure (content mismatch, missing file, extra file, missing module, unexpected module, version mismatch).  The command must exit with a non-zero status when any verification fails, and zero when everything verifies successfully.  ### FR4 — Consistency with `-mod=vendor` builds  - Commands run with `-mod=vendor` must not silently accept a `vendor/` directory that is inconsistent with `go.mod`; the existing "inconsistent vendoring" error must continue to be reported for module-list mismatches. - Verification results must be reusable: a build in vendor mode must be able to detect that the vendor tree fails verification without requiring the user to run a separate manual step, at minimum by refusing to report success on a tree that is known to be inconsistent.  ### FR5 — Backward and forward compatibility  - A `vendor/modules.txt` that lacks hash information (e.g. produced by an older Go release) must be handled gracefully: the go command must report that the vendored code **cannot be verified** (with an actionable message such as “re-run `go mod vendor` to record hashes”), rather than failing with a parse error or reporting a false success. - Modules vendored from a replacement target, and modules whose `go.sum` entry is absent, must be handled per existing `go mod` semantics and reported distinctly. - `go mod vendor` must remain idempotent and must update `vendor/modules.txt` hashes when dependencies change.  ### FR6 — Interaction with `go.sum` and other module commands  - `go mod tidy`, `go mod download`, and `go mod vendor` must keep `go.sum` and the vendored hash records in sync. - `go mod verify` in a non-vendored module must retain its current behavior (verifying the module cache) unchanged.  ## Non-Goals  - Verifying that the *main module's* own source is unmodified (there is no hash for it). - Detecting modifications to files in `vendor/` that the upstream module does not contain, beyond noting them as unexpected content affecting the module hash. - Any new cryptographic algorithm; the existing `h1:` dirhash scheme is reused. - Network-based re-verification or checksum-database queries during vendored verification.  ## Acceptance Criteria  1. In a module with dependencies, `go mod vendor` produces a `vendor/modules.txt` that contains a hash for each vendored module/version. 2. Immediately after `go mod vendor`, running `go mod verify` in that module succeeds (exit status 0) and reports that the vendored modules were verified. 3. Modifying any file under `vendor/<module>/` causes `go mod verify` to fail with a non-zero exit status, naming the affected module and file. 4. Deleting a file under `vendor/<module>/` causes verification to fail and identify the missing file. 5. Editing a version line in `vendor/modules.txt` to a version not present in `go.mod` causes verification to fail with an "inconsistent vendoring"-style error. 6. Adding a module to `vendor/modules.txt` that is not required by `go.mod` causes verification to fail. 7. Verification completes with no network access (verifiable by running with `GOPROXY=off` / `GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor` in an isolated environment). 8. A `vendor/modules.txt` produced by an older Go release (no hashes) produces a clear, non-fatal-to-parse diagnostic stating that vendored code cannot be verified and suggesting `go mod vendor`, and does not report a false success. 9. A repository whose `vendor/` was produced by the new `go mod vendor` still builds successfully with an older Go toolchain (unknown metadata is ignored).  ## Open Questions for Design Review  - Should verification be the default behavior of `go mod verify` in vendor mode, or exposed via an explicit flag/subcommand (e.g. `go mod verify -mod=vendor`)? - Should `-mod=vendor` builds verify hashes by default, or only check `modules.txt`/`go.mod` consistency (for performance on large trees)? - Should per-file hashes be recorded (allowing precise file-level diffs) in addition to the module-level `h1:` hash?

issue_title: cmd/go: allow serving module under the subdirectory of git repository
requirement: The `go` command shall support Go modules located in subdirectories of Git repositories, allowing import paths of the form `host/repository/subdirectory` where the repository root does not contain a `go.mod` file. The command shall resolve such imports by cloning the parent repository at `host/repository`, locating the `go.mod` file within the specified `subdirectory`, and validating that the declared module path matches the full import path. It shall support semantic version tags formatted as `subdirectory/vX.Y.Z` for subdirectory modules and ensure that module operations including `go get`, `go build`, `go mod download`, and `go mod tidy` correctly fetch, verify, and compile subdirectory modules without requiring the repository root to be a valid Go module, while maintaining compatibility with GOPROXY and direct VCS fetching modes.

issue_title: [web] Support compute on separate thread in Flutter Web
requirement: **Requirement: Off-Main-Thread Execution for `compute` in Flutter Web**  Flutter Web shall execute work submitted through `compute()` on a separate thread, using Web Workers as the background execution mechanism, so that CPU-intensive callbacks do not block the main UI thread.  **Functional requirements**  1. `compute(callback, message)` on Flutter Web shall run `callback` in a Web Worker rather than synchronously on the main thread. 2. The `message` argument and the returned result shall be transferred between the main thread and the worker. Values that cannot be sent across the worker boundary shall produce a clear, documented error. 3. The public `compute` API signature and return type shall remain unchanged, so existing code runs without modification. 4. The callback passed to `compute` shall be a top-level or static function, consistent with the existing contract on other platforms. Closures that capture state shall be rejected with a descriptive error. 5. Errors thrown in the worker shall propagate to the caller's `Future` as errors, with the original message and stack trace where available. 6. Worker lifecycle shall be managed by the framework: workers shall be created on demand, reused from a pool where practical, and terminated when no longer needed or when the application is disposed. 7. If Web Workers are unavailable in the runtime environment, `compute` shall fall back to the current main-thread behavior and emit a debug-mode warning.  **Non-functional requirements**  8. Main-thread responsiveness: while a `compute` callback runs, the main thread shall continue to process frames and input events. This shall be verified by a test that runs a long computation and confirms frame callbacks continue to fire. 9. Compatibility: the behavior shall be supported on the browsers Flutter Web officially targets, and shall work with both the CanvasKit and HTML renderers. 10. Serialization overhead shall be documented, and large payloads should be transferable (e.g., `ArrayBuffer`) where the data type permits.  **Acceptance criteria**  - A unit or integration test runs a CPU-bound function via `compute` on web and verifies that it executes in a worker context, not the main thread. - A test confirms that the UI remains responsive (frames continue to render) during a long-running `compute` call. - Existing `compute` tests pass on web without modification. - Documentation for `compute` is updated to describe web behavior, restrictions on callbacks and message types, and the fallback path.

issue_title: Implement a code formatter for GDScript in the script editor
requirement: The script editor shall provide a built-in GDScript code formatter that reformats the active GDScript file to conform to the official GDScript style guide. The formatter shall be invocable manually via a menu command and a user-configurable keyboard shortcut, and shall optionally run automatically on file save when enabled in Editor Settings. It shall normalize indentation (tabs or spaces according to user preference), spacing around operators and delimiters, blank-line usage between functions and classes, and line structure, while preserving the code's semantic behavior, string literals, and comment content. When a text selection exists, the formatter shall apply only to the selected lines; otherwise it shall format the entire file. If the script contains syntax errors, the formatter shall leave the code unmodified and display an informative message to the user. All formatting actions shall be reversible through the standard undo/redo mechanism.
