issue_title: x/crypto: add BLAKE3 support
requirement: ## Software Requirement Specification  **Requirement ID:** XCRYPTO-BLAKE3-001 **Title:** BLAKE3 hash function support in `golang.org/x/crypto` **Source:** Informal feature request: "x/crypto: add BLAKE3 support" **Type:** Functional  ### Requirement Statement  The `golang.org/x/crypto` module SHALL provide a new package, `golang.org/x/crypto/blake3`, implementing the BLAKE3 cryptographic hash function in full conformance with the official BLAKE3 specification (v1.0 or later) and its published test vectors.  ### Functional Requirements  1. **Hashing API.** The package SHALL provide an interface consistent with existing `x/crypto` hash packages (e.g., `blake2b`, `sha3`), including at minimum:    - a constructor returning an implementation of `hash.Hash` with the default 32-byte digest size;    - a one-shot convenience function equivalent to `Sum256(data)`.  2. **Modes of operation.** The package SHALL support all modes defined by the BLAKE3 specification:    - plain hashing (default 32-byte output);    - extendable output (XOF) — arbitrary-length output with the ability to continue generating output bytes;    - keyed hashing with a 32-byte key (MAC usage);    - key derivation mode with a caller-supplied context string.  3. **Streaming semantics.** Incremental hashing via `io.Writer`-style updates SHALL produce results identical to one-shot hashing for all input sizes and update patterns, including empty input.  4. **Portability.** The package SHALL include a pure-Go portable implementation. Architecture-optimized backends (e.g., AVX2, SSE4.1, NEON) MAY be provided; when present, backend selection SHALL be automatic at build time, SHALL fall back to the portable core on unsupported platforms, and all backends SHALL produce bit-identical outputs.  5. **Correctness verification.** The implementation SHALL pass the complete official BLAKE3 test-vector suite (unkeyed, keyed, and key-derivation modes; all specified input and output lengths) for every supported backend, verified in CI.  6. **API quality.** The public API SHALL be idiomatic Go, fully documented with GoDoc, free of `go vet` and staticcheck findings, and designed for long-term stability consistent with the Go compatibility guidelines applicable to `x/crypto`.  ### Non-Functional Requirements  1. The package SHALL NOT introduce dependencies outside the Go standard library. 2. The package SHALL build and pass its test suite on all GOOS/GOARCH platforms in the project's CI matrix. 3. Benchmarks SHALL be provided; optimized backends SHALL be validated by cross-checking against the pure-Go implementation. 4. Documentation SHALL describe the security properties and intended usage of each mode and SHALL reference the BLAKE3 specification.  ### Acceptance Criteria  - All official BLAKE3 test vectors pass for all modes on all supported platforms and backends. - The API design is reviewed and approved by `x/crypto` maintainers. - CI passes (build, tests, vet/lint) across the supported platform matrix. - GoDoc documentation is complete for all exported identifiers.  ### Constraints  - Package path: `golang.org/x/crypto/blake3`. - Conformance target: BLAKE3 specification v1.0+ and official test vectors. - License: BSD-3-Clause, consistent with the Go project. - Out of scope: FIPS 140 validation; inclusion in the standard library `crypto` package; third-party API wrappers.

issue_title: x/crypto: add BLAKE3 support
requirement: **Requirement: Add BLAKE3 Hash Function Support to golang.org/x/crypto**  The `golang.org/x/crypto` module shall provide an implementation of the BLAKE3 cryptographic hash function, exposed through a public API consistent with existing hash packages in the module (e.g., `blake2b`, `blake2s`, `sha3`).  **Functional Requirements**  1. **Hash interface compliance:** The package shall implement `hash.Hash` so that `Write`, `Sum`, `Reset`, `Size`, and `BlockSize` behave as defined by the `hash.Hash` contract. 2. **Default output length:** The default digest size shall be 32 bytes (256 bits). 3. **Extendable output (XOF):** The package shall provide an extendable-output mode that produces arbitrary-length output via a reader interface (e.g., `io.Reader`), without requiring the caller to specify the length in advance. 4. **Keyed hashing:** The package shall support keyed hashing using a 32-byte key, producing a MAC-equivalent output. 5. **Key derivation:** The package shall support key derivation mode with a caller-supplied context string, per the BLAKE3 specification. 6. **Incremental hashing:** The package shall support streaming input of arbitrary size through repeated `Write` calls, producing identical output regardless of how input is chunked. 7. **Parallelism:** The implementation shall correctly process input in 1 KiB chunks organized in a Merkle tree structure as specified by BLAKE3. Optional parallelism (e.g., via goroutines) may be provided but shall not alter output. 8. **Test vectors:** The implementation shall pass the official BLAKE3 test vectors, including hash, keyed hash, and derive-key modes across all input lengths in the official test suite.  **Non-Functional Requirements**  9. **Conformance:** Output shall match the official BLAKE3 specification (https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3-specs) bit-for-bit. 10. **Performance:** Portable pure-Go implementation shall be provided. Architecture-specific assembly optimizations (e.g., AVX2, AVX-512, SSE4.1, NEON) are optional and shall fall back to the portable implementation when unavailable. 11. **Constant-time behavior:** Keyed hashing and key derivation shall not leak key material through timing side channels. 12. **Dependencies:** The implementation shall depend only on the Go standard library and existing `golang.org/x/...` packages, with no cgo requirement. 13. **Documentation:** Each exported identifier shall have GoDoc documentation, and the package shall include runnable examples for hashing, keyed hashing, key derivation, and XOF usage. 14. **Compatibility:** The package shall support all Go versions currently supported by the `golang.org/x/crypto` module.  **Acceptance Criteria**  - All official BLAKE3 test vectors pass in CI on amd64, arm64, and 386. - Fuzz tests confirm that incremental and one-shot hashing produce identical results. - Benchmarks are included for hashing inputs of 64 B, 1 KiB, 64 KiB, and 1 MiB.

issue_title: Feature request: Use 'trampolines' to make most of the body of a generic function non-generic
requirement: **REQ-101: Generic Function Trampolining for Non-Generic Function Bodies**  **Requirement Statement:** The compiler shall restructure the lowering of generic functions such that a minimal, generated generic entry stub (a "trampoline") performs generic parameter resolution exactly once per invocation and transfers control—preferably via tail call—to a non-generic implementation function containing the majority of the original function body.  **Sub-requirements:**  - **REQ-101.1:** For each generic function, the compiler shall generate a trampoline stub whose sole responsibility is to capture the generic context (type/metadata parameters) and forward the call, together with all original arguments and resolved metadata, to the non-generic implementation. - **REQ-101.2:** The trampoline shall contain no logic beyond generic dispatch and argument forwarding; all remaining function logic shall reside in the non-generic implementation. - **REQ-101.3:** The non-generic implementation shall be emitted as a single shared body parameterized by runtime type metadata, rather than duplicated once per generic instantiation. - **REQ-101.4:** Observable behavior—including return values, side effects, exception/error propagation, dynamic dispatch results, and specialization semantics—shall remain identical to the current generic execution model. - **REQ-101.5:** The trampoline shall preserve debuggability by producing correct stack traces and profiling/profiler-attribution frames for both the trampoline and the implementation function. - **REQ-101.6:** The public API and calling convention for invoking generic functions shall remain unchanged; modifications shall be confined to internal compilation and call paths.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  1. All existing conformance and regression tests pass without modification. 2. The function body (excluding the trampoline) is emitted exactly once per generic function, independent of the number of instantiations. 3. Generic dispatch overhead is incurred only at trampoline entry; no generic re-dispatch occurs within the function body. 4. Benchmark suites show no performance regression exceeding the established threshold, and per-instantiation code size is measurably reduced. 5. Debug and profiling output correctly identifies the trampoline and implementation frames.

requirement: **REQ-WIN-PV-001: PlatformView Support for Windows**  The system shall provide the capability to embed native Windows UI components (PlatformViews) within the application's rendering surface, enabling seamless composition of native Windows controls with application-rendered content.  **Functional Requirements:** - **FR-1:** The system shall expose an API to create, register, and manage native Windows views (backed by HWND or Windows Composition visuals) using a unique identifier. - **FR-2:** The system shall composite native view content into the application frame via a texture-based or composition-based rendering path compatible with the Windows graphics stack (DirectX/DirectComposition). - **FR-3:** The system shall implement accurate hit-testing and input routing to deliver mouse, keyboard, touch, and pointer events to the appropriate native view or application layer, including proper focus management. - **FR-4:** The system shall manage the full lifecycle of PlatformViews—initialization, layout updates (resize, reposition), and disposal—ensuring proper cleanup of native resources and handles. - **FR-5:** The system shall support multiple simultaneous PlatformViews with correct z-ordering, clipping, and transparency relative to other application content.  **Constraints:** - Target platforms: Windows 10 (build 17763 / version 1809) and later, including Windows 11. - Implementation must integrate with the existing Windows message loop and windowing architecture without blocking the UI thread.  **Acceptance Criteria:** 1. Native Windows controls (e.g., WebView2, custom Win32 controls) render visibly and correctly within the application window. 2. User interactions (clicks, text input, gestures) are correctly captured by the embedded native view and do not leak to underlying application widgets. 3. PlatformViews resize, reposition, and clip correctly in response to application window resizing and layout changes. 4. No memory leaks, handle leaks, or crashes occur during repeated creation and destruction of PlatformViews. 5. Rendering performance remains stable with PlatformViews present, maintaining target frame rates without visible jank during scrolling or resizing.

issue_title: [web] Support compute on separate thread in Flutter Web
requirement: **REQ-WEB-COMPUTE-001: Multi-threaded Compute Support for Flutter Web**  **Overview:** Enable the `compute` function in Flutter Web to execute callbacks on a separate thread using Web Workers, preventing UI thread blocking during intensive computations while maintaining API compatibility with non-web platforms.  **Functional Requirements:** 1. The `compute<T, R>(FutureOr<R> Function(T message) callback, T message)` function shall execute the `callback` within a dedicated Web Worker instance rather than on the main thread. 2. Input data (`message`) shall be transferred to the worker via `postMessage` using structured clone semantics, with support for Transferable Objects (e.g., `ArrayBuffer`, `ByteData`) to enable zero-copy transfer of binary data. 3. Results computed in the worker shall be posted back to the main thread and used to resolve the returned `Future<R>`. 4. Exceptions thrown within the worker callback shall be serialized, transmitted to the main thread, and re-thrown to reject the returned Future with the original error type and stack trace where possible. 5. Worker instances shall be automatically terminated and dereferenced upon task completion (success or failure) to prevent memory leaks. 6. The system shall support concurrent execution of multiple simultaneous `compute` invocations, each utilizing a separate worker instance up to browser or configured limits.  **Technical Constraints:** - Must utilize the standard Web Workers API; target browser support includes Chrome 80+, Firefox 78+, Safari 14+, and Edge 80+. - Implementation must address the inability to directly serialize Dart function closures to workers by employing a worker entry-point strategy (e.g., worker loads the compiled Dart module and invokes callbacks via a function registry or generated bootstrap code). - Must comply with Content Security Policy (CSP) restrictions; worker scripts must be loadable from origins permitted by the `worker-src` or `script-src` directives. - Must not require modifications to the public API signature of `compute` in `package:flutter/foundation.dart`.  **Non-Functional Requirements:** - **Performance:** The UI thread must maintain <16ms frame times during compute operations; IPC overhead shall not exceed 10% of total execution time for tasks exceeding 100ms. - **Resource Management:** The system shall enforce a maximum concurrent worker limit (default: minimum of browser limit or 4 workers) to prevent resource exhaustion. - **Reliability:** Unhandled errors or crashes within workers shall not terminate the main application; all errors must surface as Future rejections on the main thread.  **Acceptance Criteria:** 1. [ ] Executing `compute` with a CPU-intensive task (e.g., parsing a 50MB JSON string) does not block the UI thread (verified via concurrent 60fps animation rendering). 2. [ ] The returned Future resolves with the correct result value matching synchronous execution. 3. [ ] Throwing an exception inside the compute callback causes the Future to reject with the corresponding exception on the main thread. 4. [ ] Transferring a 10MB `Uint8List` to the worker utilizes Transferable Objects (verified by buffer neutering on the main thread post-transfer). 5. [ ] Executing 100 sequential `compute` calls results in no detectable memory growth (verified via browser DevTools heap snapshots showing worker cleanup). 6. [ ] The feature functions correctly under strict CSP headers that restrict workers to `'self'` only. 7. [ ] Multiple concurrent `compute` calls (e.g., 3 simultaneous) execute in parallel without deadlock or race conditions.  **Dependencies:** - Requires `flutter build web` toolchain support to emit worker-compatible JavaScript bundles and worker bootstrap scripts. - No breaking changes to existing `compute` usage in application code.

issue_title: Statically checked tensor shapes
requirement: **Requirement: Statically Checked Tensor Shapes**  The library shall verify tensor shape compatibility at compile time (or, where static analysis is not possible, at the earliest feasible point before execution) so that shape mismatches in tensor operations are detected and reported before runtime computation begins.  **Details:**  1. **Shape encoding:** Tensor shapes shall be representable in the type system or in a static analysis pass, including rank (number of dimensions) and, where known, the size of each dimension. 2. **Operation checking:** Every tensor operation (e.g., arithmetic, matrix multiplication, reshape, concatenation, reduction, and broadcasting) shall have a shape rule that is checked statically. Invalid combinations shall produce a compile-time error identifying the operation, the expected shapes, and the actual shapes. 3. **Symbolic and dynamic dimensions:** The system shall support symbolic (named or generic) dimensions so that functions can be written polymorphically over shapes. Dimensions unknown until runtime shall be tracked as unknown and checked at runtime only where static verification is impossible, with the runtime check producing an error equivalent in clarity to the static one. 4. **Broadcasting:** Broadcasting rules shall be applied and validated statically when operand shapes are known. 5. **Error reporting:** Diagnostics shall be human-readable and indicate the source location of the mismatched operation. 6. **Compatibility:** Existing dynamically shaped code shall continue to work; static shape checking shall be opt-in or degrade gracefully to dynamic checks when shapes are not annotated. 7. **Performance:** Static shape checking shall incur no runtime overhead for operations whose shapes are fully verified at compile time.

issue_title: Feature Request: Easier to extend base RNN implementation
requirement: **Requirement: Extensible Base RNN Implementation**  The base RNN implementation shall be designed so that developers can create custom recurrent architectures by subclassing and overriding well-defined extension points, without modifying or duplicating the core library code.  **Functional requirements**  1. The base RNN class shall expose separate, overridable methods for:    - Initializing the hidden state (including zero, random, and user-supplied initial states).    - Computing a single time-step update (the recurrent cell computation).    - Processing a full input sequence, including handling of batch-first and time-first layouts.    - Producing the output from hidden states, with the default producing the per-step outputs and final state. 2. Subclasses shall be able to replace the recurrent cell computation alone while reusing the base class's sequence iteration, state handling, and masking logic. 3. The base class shall support registering or passing a custom cell module so that new cell types (e.g., GRU-like or LSTM-like variants) can be used without subclassing the full RNN. 4. Parameters defined in custom cells shall be automatically registered, tracked, and included in the model's parameter collection, saving, and loading routines. 5. The base class shall validate overridden methods' input and output shapes and raise a descriptive error when an extension returns tensors of incompatible shape. 6. Extension points shall be documented with their expected signatures, argument types, shape conventions, and an example of a minimal custom subclass.  **Non-functional requirements**  7. Adding the extension hooks shall not change the output or numerical results of existing built-in RNN, LSTM, and GRU implementations (verified by existing regression tests). 8. Performance of built-in models shall not degrade by more than 5% in benchmark runs after the refactor. 9. Backward compatibility shall be maintained: existing user code that subclasses the base RNN or calls its public methods shall continue to work, with any deprecations announced at least one minor release in advance.  **Acceptance criteria**  10. A test suite includes at least one custom subclass that overrides only the cell computation, and it trains and runs inference successfully. 11. A test suite includes a custom cell with learnable parameters, verifying that those parameters appear in the model's parameter list, receive gradients, and round-trip through save and load. 12. Documentation includes a tutorial section demonstrating how to implement a custom recurrent layer using the extension points.

issue_title: non-negative least squares solver feature request
requirement: ## Requirement: Non-Negative Least Squares (NNLS) Solver  ### Summary Add a solver for the non-negative least squares problem to the library, enabling users to find the vector **x** that minimizes the residual ‖**Ax** − **b**‖₂ subject to the constraint **x** ≥ 0 (element-wise).  ### Motivation Currently, users needing constrained least-squares solutions must implement their own active-set or projected-gradient routines, or apply workarounds (e.g., clipping negative results, which yields suboptimal fits). A built-in, numerically robust NNLS solver removes this gap and supports constrained regression tasks such as non-negative component analysis, curve fitting with non-negative coefficients, and bounded unmixing.  ### Functional Requirements  **1. Public API** Provide a callable exposed at the top level of the package, e.g.:  ``` nnls(A, b, *, max_iter=None, tol=1e-10) -> NNLSResult ```  - `A`: 2-D array-like of shape (m, n) containing the design matrix (real-valued). - `b`: 1-D array-like of shape (m,) containing the right-hand side. - `max_iter`: optional maximum number of active-set iterations (default: at least 3·n). - `tol`: optional convergence tolerance for the optimality/KKT conditions.  **2. Result** Return a result object (named-tuple-like) exposing at least: - `x`: 1-D array of shape (n,) — the non-negative solution vector. - `residual`: the residual ‖**Ax** − **b**‖₂. - `rank`: effective rank of the problem (number of active/free variables in the solution). - `iterations`: number of active-set iterations performed. - `unconstrained_sol`: optional — the unconstrained least-squares solution, for comparison/diagnostics.  All returned arrays must be plain NumPy arrays with the same dtype policy as the rest of the library (float64 promotion for integer inputs).  **3. Algorithm** - Implement the classic Lawson–Hanson active-set algorithm (or an equivalent method with proven convergence) that is numerically stable and terminates. - The solution must satisfy the KKT optimality conditions: **x** ≥ 0, and **A**ᵀ(**b** − **Ax**) ≥ 0 on the zero (inactive) entries. - Support over-determined (m > n), under-determined (m < n), square, and rank-deficient systems without crashing or returning invalid values.  **4. Validation and error handling** - Raise `ValueError` when `A` is not 2-D, when `b` is not 1-D, when `len(b) != A.shape[0]`, or when either input contains NaN or infinite values. - Raise `ValueError` for non-positive or non-finite `tol`. - Never return negative values in `x` beyond floating-point noise (clip to exactly zero when below tolerance). - Never raise on convergence failure due to iteration limits; instead return the best iterate found together with a status/warning flag.  **5. Performance** - Solve a representative problem (e.g., m = n = 100, random well-conditioned dense `A`) in well under one second on typical hardware. - Memory usage must be O(m·n) with no unnecessary copies of large inputs.  **6. Documentation** - Include a docstring with the mathematical problem statement, parameter descriptions, return-value descriptions, and a usage example. - Add the solver to the public API reference/index and mention it in the relevant "optimization/least squares" documentation section, with a short example showing recovery of a known non-negative solution.  **7. Testing** - Unit tests covering: exact recovery of a known non-negative solution with noise-free data; correctness versus a brute-force/reference solution; case where the unconstrained solution contains negative components (the constrained result must have strictly lower or equal residual and non-negative entries); rank-deficient input; m < n input; underdetermined/ill-conditioned input; random validation against an independent reference implementation over many seeds; input-validation error cases; and iteration-limit behavior.  ### Non-Goals - Support for additional constraints (equality, box bounds) or sparse matrix inputs in the initial version. - Support for complex-valued inputs. - L1/regularized (e.g., LASSO) variants.

issue_title: Add a Trait system for GDScript
requirement: # Requirement: Trait System for GDScript  **Component:** GDScript language (Godot Engine) **Type:** Language feature — new first-class declaration form (`trait`) **Priority:** Proposed (design phase; requires RFC approval before implementation)  ---  ## 1. Overview  GDScript shall provide a **Trait** system: a language construct that allows a set of members (constants, variables, properties, signals, and methods, with optional default implementations) to be defined once and then *applied* ("mixed in") to one or more classes, without those classes inheriting from a common base class.  Traits address the recurring OOP problems in Godot projects of:  - **Code duplication** — the same behaviour (e.g. `fly()`, `take_damage()`, `save_to_disk()`) re-implemented in unrelated node types. - **Lack of multiple inheritance** — a class cannot extend two classes, so shared behaviour must be duplicated or forced into an artificial common base class that produces deep, hard-to-maintain inheritance chains. - **Poorly scoped shared contracts** — "interface-like" behaviour is currently expressed as bare scripts extended from (which brings base-class semantics, constructor coupling and member-collision behaviour) or as documentation conventions only. - **Unenforceable contracts** — a convention such as "every `Actor` must implement `die()`" is not checked by the compiler or editor.  ## 2. Terminology  | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **Trait** | A named, reusable bundle of members that can be applied to a class. Declared with the `trait` keyword. | | **Trait body** | The block of members declared inside a trait. | | **Applying / using a trait** | Associating one or more traits with a class definition. | | **Trait requirement** | A member declared in a trait *without* a body (an abstract contract). | | **Trait default implementation** | A member declared in a trait *with* a body, providing a fallback implementation for applying classes that do not override it. | | **Linearization** | The deterministic ordering used to resolve which trait supplies a member when multiple applied traits provide it. | | **Qualified call** | Explicitly selecting a member from a specific trait, e.g. `Flyable.fly()` or `super(TraitName)`. |  ## 3. Scope  ### 3.1 In scope (MVP)  1. Declaring traits in `.gd` files (top-level and nested inside another class/script). 2. Declaring trait members: constants, `var`, `@export` variables, properties, signals, methods, and `static` members. 3. Abstract requirements (no body) and default implementations (with body) for trait methods. 4. Applying traits to class definitions, with and without overriding trait members. 5. Trait composition (a trait may use other traits). 6. Compile-time validation: unimplemented requirements, conflicting members, duplicate application, cyclic composition. 7. Type checking: trait members participate in the class's static type information, and type inference works through applied traits. 8. Editor support: trait declarations are visible in the script editor / "Members" dock; applying a trait is visible in the class's member list. 9. Full documentation in the GDScript reference manual plus at least one official example project.  ### 3.2 Out of scope (MVP / explicitly deferred)  - Traits as runtime *values* (e.g. passing a trait as an argument, `is` checks against a trait, dynamic trait application at runtime). Traits are a **compile-time** construct in the MVP. - Applying traits to objects/instances at runtime (`obj.add_trait(...)`). - Modifying `class_name` registration semantics — a trait may register a `class_name` for tooling purposes but is not instantiable. - Generics, higher-kinded types, or associated types on traits (may be considered in a follow-up RFC). - Changes to the GDScript bytecode format beyond what is strictly necessary (see §7).  ---  ## 4. Functional Requirements  ### 4.1 Trait declaration  - **FR-1.1** GDScript shall support a `trait` declaration at the top level of a script file and as a nested declaration inside a class.    ```gdscript   trait Flyable:       var max_speed: float = 300.0       signal took_off        func fly() -> void:            # requirement (no body)           pass        func land() -> void:            # default implementation           velocity = Vector2.ZERO    class Bird extends Node2D:       use Flyable:                   # see §4.3           func fly() -> void:               ...   ```  - **FR-1.2** A trait declaration shall have the form `trait <Identifier> [extends <BaseTrait>[, <BaseTrait>...]]:` followed by an indented member block. The body may be empty. - **FR-1.3** A trait **shall not** be instantiable: `Flyable.new()` shall be a compile-time error with a dedicated diagnostic message. - **FR-1.4** A trait **may** declare `class_name`, allowing the trait to be referenced by its global class name from other scripts, exactly as a class is. - **FR-1.5** A trait **shall not** extend a `Node`/native class or a user class. It may only extend other traits (§4.5). Attempting to extend a non-trait shall produce a compile-time error. - **FR-1.6** A trait **may** be declared in a script that also declares a class; both forms shall coexist in the same file.  ### 4.2 Trait members  - **FR-2.1** A trait body may declare: `const`, `var`, `@export var`, `@onready var`, `signal`, `func`, `static func`, `static var`, and `@export` categories/groups annotations. - **FR-2.2** A trait member declared **without** a body (methods only) is a **requirement**: every applying class must supply an implementation. For `var`/`const`/`signal` declarations, a value/initialiser is optional; an omitted initialiser means the applying class must provide the initial value (or the member is left at its default zero value and the class is not required to override it — see FR-2.3). - **FR-2.3** Applying classes **may** override any trait member (variables, constants, signals, methods) by declaring a member with the same name. An override must be type-compatible with the trait declaration (same or narrower type for `var`/`const` return values; identical or covariant parameter types); incompatible overrides shall be a compile-time error. - **FR-2.4** A trait method **with** a body provides a **default implementation** used by applying classes that do not override it. The default implementation's `self` refers to the applying class instance, and it may access the applying class's members and other applied traits' members. - **FR-2.5** Within a trait default implementation, `super` shall resolve to the next implementation in the linearization order of the applying class (§4.6), enabling cooperative behaviour. `super()` calls with no arguments and `super(args)` calls shall both be supported. - **FR-2.6** A trait member shall not be marked `abstract` in the MVP; absence of a body implies requirement semantics. - **FR-2.7** Members declared in a trait shall appear in the applying class's member list at runtime and in the editor, with a visible indicator (e.g. an icon/label) that the member originates from a trait.  ### 4.3 Applying traits  - **FR-3.1** A class definition shall be able to apply one or more traits via a `use` clause:    ```gdscript   class Bird extends Node2D use Flyable, Damageable:       func fly() -> void: ...   ```    and via an indented block form that permits inline overriding:    ```gdscript   class Bird extends Node2D:       use Flyable:           func fly() -> void: ...       use Damageable   ```    The two forms shall be equivalent; the block form shall be required if any trait member is to be overridden inline.  - **FR-3.2** The `use` clause shall appear after the `extends` clause and before the class body, and shall accept a comma-separated list of trait references (global `class_name`, local identifier, or `"res://path.gd"` script path). - **FR-3.3** Applying a trait shall merge the trait's members into the class as if they had been declared in the class, subject to the resolution rules of §4.6. - **FR-3.4** Applying a trait shall **not** change the class's base class, and shall not introduce an implicit base class in the inheritance hierarchy. - **FR-3.5** The same trait may be applied to any number of classes, including classes in different scripts, and the same trait may be applied to nested/inner classes. - **FR-3.6** A class shall not apply the same trait twice (directly or transitively) — duplicate application shall be detected and reported as an error, unless the duplicate arises solely through composition and is resolved by linearization (§4.5.3). - **FR-3.7** Applying traits to a class that is itself extended by other classes shall work; the trait members are inherited by subclasses like normal class members. - **FR-3.8** Trait application shall be permitted on classes with `@tool` annotation and on scripts used as resources.  ### 4.4 Requirements enforcement  - **FR-4.1** If an applying class does not provide an implementation for a trait requirement, the compiler shall emit an error identifying the trait, the member, and the class. - **FR-4.2** If a requirement is satisfied by another applied trait (directly or transitively), that shall be accepted — no error. - **FR-4.3** Requirement checks shall be performed statically at parse/compile time and reported with the source location of the offending class.  ### 4.5 Trait composition  - **FR-5.1** A trait may apply other traits using the same `use` syntax:    ```gdscript   trait Mobile:       use Flyable       func move(dir: Vector2) -> void: ...   ```  - **FR-5.2** A trait's own requirements and default implementations shall be propagated to applying classes. - **FR-5.3** If two composed traits both provide a member with the same name and no unambiguous resolution exists (§4.6), the compiler shall emit a **conflict error** naming both traits and the member. - **FR-5.4** Cyclic trait composition (trait A uses B, B uses A, directly or transitively) shall be detected and reported as a compile-time error with a diagnostic showing the cycle. - **FR-5.5** A trait may apply a trait that itself applies other traits; composition shall be flattened at compile time.  ### 4.6 Member resolution and linearization  - **FR-6.1** Resolution order for a member name shall be:   1. Members declared directly in the class body (highest priority).   2. Members supplied by applied traits, in **reverse linearization order** (last applied wins), where the linearization is computed over the class's base class and the full transitive closure of applied traits.   3. Members inherited from the base class.   4. Members inherited from native/engine base classes (lowest priority). - **FR-6.2** When two applied traits provide the same member name and neither is preferred by linearization order (i.e. the traits are unrelated in the composition graph), the compiler shall emit a conflict error. The error message shall suggest resolution techniques. - **FR-6.3** A conflict shall be resolvable by the class by declaring the member explicitly in the class body (highest priority), thereby overriding both traits. - **FR-6.4** A class shall be able to explicitly invoke a specific trait's implementation using a qualified call:    ```gdscript   Flyable.fly()      # calls Flyable's implementation explicitly   ```    Qualified calls shall work for methods, and shall also provide a read/write path for trait-provided variables (e.g. `Flyable.max_speed`). - **FR-6.5** Method overriding in a trait-provided default implementation shall respect the standard GDScript override rules: the applying class's override replaces the trait's default, and `super` inside the trait's default reaches the next implementation in the linearization. - **FR-6.6** Signals declared in traits shall be emitted on the instance and be connectable/disconnectable normally. Connecting to a trait signal before/after instantiation shall behave as with class-declared signals. - **FR-6.7** `@export` variables from traits shall be exposed in the inspector with the trait's export hints, and shall appear under the trait's name in the inspector category if specified. - **FR-6.8** `static` members of a trait shall be accessible on the applying class (`MyClass.helper()`) and via the trait's global name (`Flyable.helper()`), and shall not be duplicated per instance.  ### 4.7 Typing and static analysis  - **FR-7.1** Trait members shall participate fully in the class's static type information: `var b: Bird = ...; b.fly()` shall type-check if `Flyable` is applied to `Bird`, and shall be a compile-time error if not. - **FR-7.2** The static type of a trait-provided member shall be the trait's declared type, unless overridden with a narrower type in the applying class. - **FR-7.3** The GDScript type checker shall be able to infer the type of a class that applies traits from a trait reference. - **FR-7.4** Assigning a class instance to a variable typed as a trait shall be permitted **only if** the trait is treated as an interface. MVP decision: traits used purely as type annotations shall be supported for classes that apply them, with the caveat documented (see §9, Open Question OQ-1). Alternatively, traits shall be usable as type hints only in "structural" mode — the MVP shall implement nominal typing: a value of type `Bird` is assignable to a variable typed `Flyable` only if `Bird` applies `Flyable`. - **FR-7.5** Documentation comments (`##`) on trait members shall be propagated to the applying class's generated documentation and shown in the editor's member list. - **FR-7.6** The type checker shall support `is` checks against traits: `if obj is Flyable:` shall be valid and evaluate to `true` when `obj`'s class applies `Flyable` (nominally, via the class's trait list at compile time).  ### 4.8 Runtime semantics  - **FR-8.1** Trait members shall be initialized as part of the applying class's member initialisation, in the order defined by the linearization (trait-provided members before base-class members unless the class body overrides them), so that trait defaults referencing other trait members are valid. - **FR-8.2** Trait-provided instance variables shall be stored on the instance in the same way as class-declared variables (no separate storage, no per-instance copies of the trait). - **FR-8.3** A class applying traits shall report the traits in its class metadata (e.g. `get_class_trait_list()`), enabling tooling and `is` checks. - **FR-8.4** `Object.get_script().get_base_script()`, resource loading, `PackedScene` round-tripping and `class_name` global registration shall be unaffected by trait application. - **FR-8.5** `duplicate()`, `duplicate()` of nodes with trait-applied scripts, and `Object.set_script()` shall preserve trait-derived behaviour (i.e. behaviour follows the script, not the instance). - **FR-8.6** Traits shall work with `@tool` scripts and with `EditorPlugin`/`EditorScript` classes.  ### 4.9 Diagnostics  - **FR-9.1** The following conditions shall produce dedicated, actionable compile-time errors (with file, line and column):   - E_TRAIT_NOT_INSTANTIABLE — attempting to instantiate a trait.   - E_TRAIT_INVALID_BASE — trait extending a non-trait.   - E_TRAIT_MISSING_IMPLEMENTATION — unimplemented trait requirement.   - E_TRAIT_MEMBER_CONFLICT — ambiguous member from two traits.   - E_TRAIT_DUPLICATE — same trait applied twice.   - E_TRAIT_CYCLE — cyclic trait composition.   - E_TRAIT_OVERRIDE_TYPE_MISMATCH — incompatible override type.   - E_TRAIT_UNKNOWN — reference to an undeclared/unresolvable trait. - **FR-9.2** Error messages shall name the trait(s), the member, and the class involved, and shall suggest a remedy (e.g. "declare `fly()` in `Bird`, or remove `use Flyable`"). - **FR-9.3** Warnings (non-fatal) shall be emitted for: an empty trait body, a trait with only requirements never applied anywhere in the project (project-wide check, optional), and a trait requirement shadowed by an unrelated base-class member of a different signature.  ### 4.10 Editor / tooling support  - **FR-10.1** The script editor shall render `trait` declarations with a distinct icon and shall support code completion, signature help, and go-to-definition for trait members. - **FR-10.2** The "Members" dock shall list trait-provided members, grouped/annotated by their originating trait. - **FR-10.3** The inspector shall group `@export` trait variables under the trait name when the trait declares a category. - **FR-10.4** The documentation generator (`--doctool`) shall emit documentation pages for traits. - **FR-10.5** Refactoring operations that rename a trait member shall rename it in all applying classes.  ---  ## 5. Non-Functional Requirements  - **NFR-1 (Backward compatibility):** No change shall alter the behaviour of any existing valid GDScript file. The `trait` and `use` keywords shall be added as reserved words; a script using `trait` or `use` as an identifier shall be reported with a clear migration message. - **NFR-2 (Grammar extensibility):** The grammar change shall be implemented such that future additions (trait `is` checks at runtime, generic traits, associated types) do not require a redesign of the trait syntax. - **NFR-3 (Performance):** Trait application shall be resolved entirely at compile time. Runtime overhead of applying a trait shall be **zero** relative to declaring the members inline: no per-instance indirection, no runtime trait tables beyond a static list of trait names per class (for `is` checks and metadata).   - Benchmark target: a class applying 5 traits with 30 total members shall have no measurable instantiation-time regression versus the same class with the members declared inline. - **NFR-4 (Memory):** Trait bodies shall not be duplicated per applying class in memory beyond the compiled method bodies (which are shared), and instance variables shall be stored once per instance. - **NFR-5 (Code size):** The implementation (parser, analyzer, bytecode compiler) shall add no more than ~3,000 lines of new code in the language core, excluding tests and documentation. - **NFR-6 (Consistency):** The feature shall be implemented in the GDScript tokenizer, parser, analyzer/type-checker, and bytecode compiler; there shall be no "parse-only, ignored at runtime" mode. - **NFR-7 (Portability):** The feature shall behave identically on all supported platforms and in the editor and in exported projects. - **NFR-8 (Testability):** The feature shall be covered by unit tests in `modules/gdscript/tests/scripts/` (parser, analyzer, runtime) with at least 25 test cases covering the acceptance criteria in §6.  ---  ## 6. Acceptance Criteria  The feature is accepted when all of the following hold:  1. **AC-1** A trait with a method requirement applied to a class that implements it compiles and the method is callable at runtime with correct `self`. 2. **AC-2** A trait with a method requirement applied to a class that does **not** implement it fails compilation with `E_TRAIT_MISSING_IMPLEMENTATION` pointing at the class declaration. 3. **AC-3** A trait with a default implementation provides the behaviour when the class does not override it, and the class's override takes precedence when present. 4. **AC-4** `super` inside a trait default implementation invokes the base class implementation (or the next trait in linearization) with correct arguments and return value. 5. **AC-5** Two unrelated traits declaring the same member name produce `E_TRAIT_MEMBER_CONFLICT`; resolving by declaring the member in the class body removes the error and the class's implementation is used. 6. **AC-6** A qualified call `TraitName.method()` invokes that trait's implementation even when overridden by the class. 7. **AC-7** Trait composition flattens correctly: applying trait `A` that uses trait `B` gives the class all of `B`'s members and requirements. 8. **AC-8** Cyclic composition (`A` uses `B`, `B` uses `A`) produces `E_TRAIT_CYCLE`. 9. **AC-9** A trait signal is emitted and can be connected to from outside; connection/disconnection semantics match class-declared signals. 10. **AC-10** An `@export` variable declared in a trait appears in the inspector and persists its value across scene save/load. 11. **AC-11** Static type checking accepts `b.fly()` on a variable typed as a class that applies the trait, and rejects it for a class that does not. 12. **AC-12** `obj is TraitName` evaluates correctly for instances of classes that apply the trait, and `false` otherwise. 13. **AC-13** Trait-provided instance variables are initialised in the correct order and are present on the instance (`obj.get("max_speed")` returns the trait default). 14. **AC-14** A class applying a trait can be saved to a `PackedScene`, reloaded, and behaves identically. 15. **AC-15** `use` of an unknown trait name produces `E_TRAIT_UNKNOWN`. 16. **AC-16** Attempting `TraitName.new()` produces `E_TRAIT_NOT_INSTANTIABLE`. 17. **AC-17** A trait declared with `class_name` is resolvable from another script by global name and by path. 18. **AC-18** Existing GDScript test suite passes with zero regressions; no existing test file requires modification. 19. **AC-19** `--doctool` emits a documentation page for each trait. 20. **AC-20** Performance benchmark shows no measurable instantiation-time or memory regression versus inline declaration of the same members.  ---  ## 7. Implementation Notes (constraints for the implementer)  - **C-1** Tokenizer: add `trait` and `use` as keywords; add them to the keyword-completion list and to the "reserved words" documentation and the `GDScript` grammar summary. - **C-2** Parser: introduce a `TraitNode` class in `modules/gdscript/gdscript_parser.h/.cpp` analogous to `ClassNode`, and represent trait application as a list of resolved trait nodes on the class. - **C-3** Analyzer: perform trait resolution (loading the trait script, walking its `use` list, building the linearization), requirement checking, conflict detection, and override type-checking in `modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp` before normal member resolution, so that trait members are visible to the standard resolution machinery. - **C-4** Compiler: emit trait-provided methods as ordinary methods of the class's method table (sharing the compiled function body across all applying classes where possible) so that runtime dispatch is unchanged. Instance variables from traits are added to the class's member list in the linearization-determined position. - **C-5** The class's "trait list" shall be stored in the script's `GDScript` metadata (e.g. `traits` array of resolved `GDScript*`/names) to support `is` checks and `get_class_trait_list()`. - **C-6** `ClassDB`/`Script` API: add `Script.get_class_traits()` (or equivalent) to expose applied traits at runtime. - **C-7** No new opcode is required; if the bytecode format changes, the change shall be backward-compatible with existing `.gdc` files, or the version bump shall follow the project's standard policy for GDScript bytecode.  ---  ## 8. Documentation Deliverables  - **D-1** A new chapter in the GDScript reference manual: "Traits" — covering declaration, application, requirements vs. default implementations, composition, conflict resolution, `super` semantics, typing, and limitations. - **D-2** Update of the GDScript keyword list and the "What's new in Godot" page for the target release. - **D-3** At least one official example (`godot-demo-projects`) demonstrating a trait applied to three unrelated classes, including overriding and conflict resolution. - **D-4** A migration note for scripts that use `trait` or `use` as identifiers. - **D-5** Changelog entry listing the new diagnostics and their meanings.  ---  ## 9. Open Questions (to be resolved during RFC review)  - **OQ-1** Should a trait be usable as a *structural* type (duck-typed) in variable annotations, or strictly nominal (only classes that `use` the trait are assignable)? MVP implements nominal typing; structural typing is deferred. - **OQ-2** Should the keyword be `trait` (Rust/Swift-like) or `mixin` (Ruby-like)? The MVP uses `trait`; the RFC shall confirm, and the keyword may be aliased. - **OQ-3** Should `use` be the application keyword, or should traits be applied via `extends Trait1, Trait2`? MVP uses `use`; `extends` shall remain single-inheritance. - **OQ-4** Should a trait be allowed to declare `extends` of a *class* to express "requires these base behaviours"? MVP: no. - **OQ-5** Should traits be allowed to be applied to `RefCounted`/`Object`-derived native classes directly (e.g. `class MyThing extends RefCounted use Serializable:`)? MVP: yes, any class. - **OQ-6** Interaction with `class_name` and global script class registration for traits: may a trait register a global class name? MVP: yes, with the trait marked non-instantiable in the editor's "Create New" dialog.  ---  ## 10. Out-of-Metric / Explicit Non-Goals  The following shall **not** be attempted in this requirement: runtime trait attachment/detachment, traits as first-class values, generic traits, associated types, trait objects (`Trait.new()` returning a callable bundle), metaprogramming APIs for generating traits, or any change to Godot's scene/node inheritance model.

issue_title: [RFC] Add tar-based IterableDataset implementation to PyTorch
requirement: **Requirement: Tar-Based IterableDataset Implementation for PyTorch**  **Summary:** PyTorch shall provide a built-in `IterableDataset` implementation that reads samples directly from tar archives, enabling streaming, sequential access to large datasets stored as `.tar` files without requiring full extraction to the local filesystem.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. **Streaming Iteration:** The dataset shall iterate over the members of one or more tar archives sequentially, yielding one sample per iteration step without loading the entire archive into memory.  2. **Local and Remote Sources:** The dataset shall accept local file paths and, where feasible, file-like objects or URLs, so that archives can be read from local disk or remote storage through a file-like interface.  3. **Sample Grouping:** The dataset shall support grouping tar members that share a common key (e.g., filename stem) into a single sample, with the grouping rule configurable by the user (for example, by stem, by directory prefix, or by a custom key function).  4. **Decoding Hooks:** The dataset shall accept user-supplied decoder and transform callables applied per member or per grouped sample, with a sensible default that returns raw bytes.  5. **Multi-Archive Input:** The dataset shall accept a list of archive paths and iterate across them in order, with an option to shuffle archive order and to shuffle within a bounded buffer.  6. **Distributed and Worker Sharding:** The dataset shall partition archives (and, where possible, members within an archive) across `DataLoader` workers and distributed ranks so that each sample is yielded exactly once per epoch across all workers and ranks, without duplication.  7. **Resumability and Determinism:** Given a fixed seed and epoch number, the iteration order shall be deterministic and reproducible.  8. **Error Handling:** Corrupt or truncated archive members shall raise a descriptive error or be skipped according to a user-configurable policy, and the dataset shall report the archive name and member name in the error.  9. **Compression Support:** The dataset shall transparently support uncompressed `.tar` and compressed variants (`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz`) using Python's standard `tarfile` module.  **Non-Functional Requirements:**  - **Memory:** Peak memory usage shall be independent of total archive size (bounded by the shuffle buffer and a constant read buffer). - **Performance:** Sequential read throughput for uncompressed archives shall be within 10% of raw `tarfile` iteration on the same hardware. - **Compatibility:** The implementation shall conform to the `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset` interface and work with `DataLoader` in both single-process and multi-process modes. - **Documentation:** Public API shall include docstrings and a tutorial example showing usage with `DataLoader`.  **Out of Scope (initial release):**  - Writing or modifying tar archives. - Random-access (indexed) reads by sample index; an optional index file may be considered in a follow-up. - Built-in support for specific cloud storage protocols beyond what the file-like interface provides.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - Unit tests cover single archive, multiple archives, grouped samples, compressed archives, corrupt member handling, and worker/rank sharding with no duplicated or dropped samples. - A benchmark compares throughput against raw `tarfile` iteration and is included in the PR. - Iteration order is verified reproducible across runs with the same seed and epoch.

The fallback shall not cause the build to fail.  3. **Override mechanism:** Users shall be able to override the default linker selection through the existing linker configuration mechanism (e.g., linker flags, environment variables, or build configuration option), allowing explicit selection of `mold` or any other supported linker.  4. **Compatibility:** All binaries and libraries produced with `mold` as the default linker shall be functionally equivalent to those produced with the previous default linker. All existing build configurations, test suites, and CI pipelines shall pass without modification.  5. **Documentation:** Project documentation shall be updated to describe the new default linker, the automatic fallback behavior, platform support limitations, and the mechanism for overriding the linker choice.

issue_title: Subslice search
requirement: **Requirement: Subslice Search**  The system shall provide a search operation that, given a target slice (sequence) and a query subslice (contiguous subsequence), returns the position(s) at which the query occurs within the target.  **Functional requirements**  1. The search shall accept two inputs: a `haystack` slice and a `needle` subslice, both of the same element type. 2. The search shall match only contiguous elements, preserving order. Element equality shall use the element type's standard equality comparison. 3. The search shall return the zero-based index of the first occurrence of the needle, or a documented "not found" sentinel (e.g., -1) if no occurrence exists. 4. The search shall provide a variant that returns all starting indices of non-overlapping occurrences, and a variant that returns all starting indices of overlapping occurrences. The variant used shall be selectable by the caller. 5. The search shall support an optional start offset and end bound so that the caller can restrict the search to a sub-range of the haystack without copying it.  **Edge cases**  6. An empty needle shall return index 0 (or a documented equivalent) without error. 7. A needle longer than the haystack shall return "not found" without error. 8. A needle equal to the entire haystack shall return index 0. 9. Searching an empty haystack with a non-empty needle shall return "not found." 10. Inputs of mismatched element types shall be rejected at compile time where the language supports it, or with a clear error otherwise.  **Non-functional requirements**  11. The default algorithm shall run in O(n·m) worst-case time, where n is the haystack length and m is the needle length. A linear-time algorithm (e.g., KMP) shall be used when the needle is reused across multiple searches, and this option shall be documented. 12. The search shall not allocate memory proportional to the haystack length. 13. The search shall not modify the haystack or the needle. 14. The operation shall be safe for concurrent read-only use on the same haystack.  **Acceptance criteria**  - Searching `[1,2,3,4,5]` for `[3,4]` returns 2. - Searching `[1,2,1,2,1]` for `[1,2,1]` returns 0 (first match) and yields `[0, 2]` in overlapping mode and `[0]` in non-overlapping mode. - Searching `[1,2,3]` for `[4]` returns -1. - Searching with a start offset of 2 in `[1,2,3,1,2]` for `[1,2]` returns 3. - All edge cases in items 6–9 are covered by unit tests. - Documentation includes the complexity guarantees and the return-value sentinel.

issue_title: Implement PlatformView support on Windows
requirement: ## Requirement: PlatformView support on Windows  The Flutter Windows embedder must support embedding native Win32 (`HWND`) views within the Flutter widget hierarchy through the engine’s PlatformView APIs.  ### Functional requirements  - Implement the Windows platform-view contract for creating, registering, updating, and destroying platform views. - Expose Windows embedder APIs that allow plugins and applications to associate a native `HWND` with a Flutter platform-view widget. - Composite native views at the location and size assigned by Flutter, including updates caused by layout changes, scrolling, clipping, and window resizing. - Preserve the platform views’ stacking order, transparency, opacity, and clipping when views overlap. - Deliver mouse, keyboard, focus, and text-input events to the appropriate native view, with hit testing respecting stacking order. - Allow native views to be recreated or repositioned without leaking Win32 resources, handles, or engine registrations. - Synchronize platform-view state with Flutter rendering and rebuild the affected native surface when its contents change. - Report platform-view creation and registration failures through the Windows embedder’s normal error-handling mechanism. - Integrate with the framework layer so platform-view widgets can be used by applications targeting Windows.  ### Acceptance criteria  1. A Windows integration test embeds an `HWND`-backed native control in a Flutter widget and verifies that:    - the native content is visible within the widget’s bounds;    - clicking the control activates it and delivers the expected native input;    - the control follows Flutter layout and window-size changes; and    - removing the widget destroys the native view and releases its resources. 2. A test with multiple overlapping platform views verifies correct stacking, clipping, and input routing. 3. A test verifies that a native view can display and update animated content without requiring recreation. 4. Existing Windows embedder and application tests continue to pass, and applications that do not use platform views incur no additional native-view resources. 5. Public Windows embedder APIs for platform-view creation and management are documented.

issue_title: Improve the indexability (SEO) of Flutter apps on the web
requirement:
### Feature Requirement: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) and Web Indexability Support for Flutter Web #### 1. Description The Flutter Web framework and build engine shall provide native capabilities to render crawlable semantic content, manage document-level metadata, and support static pre-rendering to ensure Flutter web applications are discoverable, indexable, and rankable by modern search engine bots (e.g., Googlebot, Bingbot). #### 2. Functional Requirements * **Semantic DOM Generation:** * The framework shall map text, imagery, and navigation widgets (e.g., `Text`, `Image`, `SelectableText`) to corresponding standard HTML semantic tags (`

`–`

`, `

`, ``) in the web DOM tree alongside the rendering canvas. * The framework shall expose an explicit navigation mechanism ensuring that routing actions map to valid HTML hyperlink elements (``) with standard anchor attributes, enabling recursive crawling of internal application routes. * **Document Metadata Management:** * The framework shall provide a declarative API to set and dynamically update document head metadata per route, including: * Page titles (``) * Standard meta tags (`description`, `keywords`, `robots`) * Canonical URLs (`<link rel="canonical">`) * Open Graph and Twitter Card tags (`og:*`, `twitter:*`) * Structured data payloads (`application/ld+json`). * **Static Content Pre-rendering:** * The Flutter build toolchain (`flutter build web`) shall introduce an optional pre-rendering mode (Static Site Generation/SSG) that outputs static HTML/CSS representations containing initial route text and metadata, which hydrates into an interactive Flutter web app upon JavaScript execution. * **Sitemap and Robots Configuration:** * The build system shall provide configurable options to automatically generate a valid `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` based on registered route configurations. #### 3. Non-Functional Requirements * **Performance:** Semantic HTML generation and DOM synchronization must not introduce more than a 5% frame rate overhead or degrade the performance of CanvasKit/WebGL rendering. * **Accessibility & SEO Cohesion:** The semantic tree used for web accessibility (Assistive Technologies) must align with the crawlable DOM elements to maintain a single source of truth for semantic data. * **Crawler Compatibility:** The rendered HTML and metadata must be accessible without requiring user interaction (such as mouse movement, clicks, or scroll triggers to initialize the DOM semantics).

issue_title: Implement PlatformView support on macOS
requirement: **Requirement: Platform View Support on macOS**  The system shall support embedding native macOS platform views (NSView instances) within the application's rendered widget hierarchy, enabling developers to compose native macOS UI components (e.g., web views, video players, maps, and custom AppKit controls) directly alongside framework-rendered content.  Specifically, the system shall:  1. **View Embedding**: Provide an API that allows developers to register, create, and insert native NSView-based views into the framework's view hierarchy at a specified position, with correct z-ordering relative to framework-rendered content.  2. **Composition and Layout**: Ensure embedded platform views are correctly sized, positioned, and clipped in accordance with the layout constraints and transformations (translation, scaling, rotation, opacity) applied by the framework's widget tree.  3. **Hit Testing and Input Dispatch**: Route pointer, keyboard, and scroll input events that intersect a platform view's bounds to the native view for handling, and forward unhandled events back to the framework.  4. **Threading and Rendering**: Manage the interaction between the framework's raster/rendering pipeline and the native AppKit view hierarchy without corrupting rendering state, introducing excessive frame jitter, or requiring the framework compositor to fall back below 60 FPS in typical usage.  5. **Lifecycle Management**: Dispose of platform views deterministically when they are removed from the widget tree, releasing associated native resources and canceling any active event subscriptions.  6. **Embedding API Parity**: Expose a platform-side registration and creation API consistent with the existing platform view APIs on other supported platforms (Android and iOS), so that plugin authors can implement macOS platform view support with minimal platform-specific divergence.  7. **Accessibility**: Ensure embedded native views participate in the macOS accessibility tree and remain reachable via assistive technologies.  **Acceptance Criteria**: - A registered platform view can be instantiated from framework code and appears at the correct location, size, and stacking order within the window. - Input events over a platform view region are handled by the native view; input events outside it are handled by the framework. - Scrolling a container containing platform views moves, clips, and composites the views correctly without visual artifacts. - Removal of a platform view from the tree results in its native resources being released without leaks or crashes. - A reference plugin (e.g., a web view) can render interactive content inside a platform view on macOS.

issue_title: Implement a Rendering Compositor
requirement: **Feature Requirement: Rendering Compositor**  **Summary:** The system shall provide a rendering compositor that combines multiple independently produced visual layers into a single final frame for display.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. **Layer Management:** The compositor shall accept multiple renderable layers (surfaces or buffers), each with properties including position, size, z-order, opacity, visibility, and transform. 2. **Ordered Composition:** The compositor shall blend layers into the output frame in ascending z-order, respecting each layer's opacity and alpha channel. 3. **Dynamic Updates:** Clients shall be able to add, remove, reorder, show, hide, and update layers at runtime, with changes reflected in the next composed frame. 4. **Transforms:** The compositor shall support at minimum translation, scaling, and rotation of layers prior to composition. 5. **Damage Tracking:** The compositor shall recompose only regions of the output affected by changed layers, unless a full-frame redraw is required. 6. **Frame Synchronization:** The compositor shall present frames at the target refresh rate and avoid tearing by synchronizing with the display's vertical blank where supported. 7. **Fallback Path:** If hardware-accelerated composition is unavailable, the compositor shall fall back to a software implementation that produces equivalent output. 8. **Output Targets:** The compositor shall direct its output to a configurable target, such as a window, an offscreen buffer, or a display surface.  **Non-Functional Requirements:**  - **Performance:** Composition of up to 32 layers at 1920×1080 and 60 FPS shall complete within 16 ms per frame on reference hardware. - **Correctness:** Output pixels shall match the defined blending equations within a tolerance of one color-channel unit. - **Thread Safety:** Layer updates from application threads shall be safe to perform concurrently with composition, without requiring the caller to lock the render loop. - **Resource Management:** The compositor shall release GPU and memory resources associated with removed layers without leaking handles. - **Error Handling:** Invalid layer parameters (e.g., zero-size buffers, out-of-range opacity) shall be rejected with a descriptive error rather than causing a crash.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - A test suite demonstrates correct z-ordering, opacity blending, and transforms against reference images. - Adding, removing, and updating layers during active rendering produces no crashes or visual corruption. - Software fallback produces output matching the accelerated path within the defined tolerance. - Documentation describes the public API for layer creation, property updates, and output configuration.

issue_title: Support Firefox as a browser in flutter run
requirement: ## Requirement: Firefox as a Target Browser for `flutter run`  ### 1. Overview  `flutter run` currently supports launching a Flutter application on a limited set of browser targets (notably Chrome, and Edge on desktop platforms). Users request the ability to run and debug Flutter web applications in Mozilla Firefox, both as a locally installed desktop browser and as a headless/containerized browser for CI use, consistent with the existing experience offered for Chrome.  ### 2. Problem Statement  Flutter's web tooling (`flutter build web`, `flutter run -d chrome`, `flutter devices`) is optimized around Chromium-based browsers. As a result:  - Firefox is not reported as an available device by `flutter devices`, and cannot be selected with `flutter run -d firefox`. - Developers targeting Firefox users are unable to verify behavior, hot reload, DevTools-driven debugging, or performance characteristics in their primary non-Chromium browser. - Projects that intentionally restrict or test on non-Chromium engines (e.g., Safari/WebKit compatibility work, Gecko-specific CSS/rendering issues) have no first-party workflow and must resort to manually launching a Firefox binary against the served `web` output. - Automated test/CI pipelines that need a Gecko engine in the browser matrix have no supported path.  ### 3. Scope  #### 3.1 In Scope  1. **Device discovery** — Detect locally installed Firefox installations (Windows, macOS, Linux) and expose them to `flutter devices` / `flutter run -d <device-id>` with a clear device name and identifier (e.g., `firefox`). 2. **Launching and running** — `flutter run -d firefox` must:    - Build and serve the web application in debug mode using the existing Dart web development server (`webdevserver`).    - Launch the selected Firefox instance against the served application URL.    - Support hot reload and hot restart over the existing web hot-reload channel, with no regressions relative to the Chrome path. 3. **Debugging** — Provide a working debugging experience equivalent to the current Chrome experience: attach the Flutter/Dart VM service to the running Firefox tab, and expose DevTools (or an equivalent debugging workflow) so breakpoints, widget inspector, logging, and the debugger are usable when running in Firefox. 4. **Build support** — `flutter build web` must be able to target Gecko explicitly via a new option (e.g., `--web-renderer`/browser-target flag consistent with existing naming conventions, such as `--target-platform`/`--browser`), producing output that is valid for Gecko. Where a browser-specific compilation option is required (e.g., Gecko-specific JavaScript output or source-map settings), it must be applied. 5. **Configuration and overrides** — Support configuration via:    - `flutter config` (e.g., an enable/disable toggle for Firefox support, consistent with how other web browsers are configured).    - `flutter run` flags (e.g., `--device-user-data-dir`/profile directory, `--web-browser-flag` equivalent for passing Gecko command-line arguments such as `--headless`, `--width`, `--height`, `--remote-debugging-port`).    - Environment variables / `CHROME_EXECUTABLE`-style overrides (e.g., `FIREFOX_EXECUTABLE`) so that non-standard install locations, snap/flatpak installs, and CI-provisioned binaries can be located. 6. **Platform-specific installation guidance** — `flutter doctor` and/or `flutter devices` must report actionable, platform-appropriate messages when Firefox is not found (including Linux package names and snap/flatpak considerations), and must report a clear error when the located binary cannot be executed. 7. **Automated tests** — The Flutter repository's own test suites must include coverage for the new Firefox target at parity with existing Chrome-target coverage (unit/integration tests for device registration, launch, and build options).  #### 3.2 Out of Scope  - Bundling or downloading Firefox on behalf of the user. - Implementing a new renderer (the existing `canvaskit`/`html`/renderer-selection behavior is unchanged; Firefox support must work with all currently supported web renderers). - Firefox support for platform-native desktop, mobile, or embedded targets (Firefox for Android/iOS is not a `flutter run` target in this requirement). - Adding new Gecko-specific APIs to the Flutter framework or engine. - Changing the default browser for `flutter run` when no `-d` flag is supplied (existing defaults must remain unchanged).  ### 4. Functional Requirements  | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | FR-1 | `flutter devices` MUST list locally installed Firefox instances as available devices, with a stable device identifier and a descriptive name that includes the browser name and, where useful, the version. | | FR-2 | `flutter run -d <firefox-device-id>` MUST build the app for the web, start the development server, and launch Firefox pointed at the served URL. | | FR-3 | Hot reload and hot restart MUST function when running in Firefox, with terminal output and error reporting consistent with other web targets. | | FR-4 | The Dart VM service MUST be reachable and debuggable when the app is running in Firefox, and `flutter attach` to a running Firefox instance MUST work. | | FR-5 | `flutter build web` MUST accept an explicit Gecko/Firefox target option and MUST produce a deployable artifact set. | | FR-6 | Firefox launch flags MUST be configurable per-run and persistable via `flutter config`; a user-specified Firefox profile/data directory MUST be honored and not deleted by the tool. | | FR-7 | If Firefox is not installed, is not executable, or fails to launch, the tool MUST emit a clear, actionable error message and exit with a non-zero status; it MUST NOT hang or silently fall back to another browser. | | FR-8 | Firefox device discovery MUST be implemented in a platform-aware manner that does not break device enumeration on Windows, macOS, or Linux, and MUST be resilient to unusual filesystem permissions and sandboxed install layouts. | | FR-9 | Existing Chrome/Edge/web workflows MUST NOT regress; all pre-existing web-related tests MUST continue to pass. |  ### 5. Non-Functional Requirements  - **Consistency:** The user experience, flags, output text, and error formats MUST match the conventions already established for Chrome, so that documentation and muscle memory transfer. - **Performance:** Browser discovery MUST NOT measurably slow down `flutter devices` or `flutter run` startup (e.g., via caching or lazy/asynchronous detection). - **Portability:** The implementation MUST work on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and MUST compile and pass tests on all supported host platforms. - **Testability:** New logic MUST be unit-testable via dependency injection/abstraction of process execution and filesystem probing, and MUST include tests for the "browser not found" and "browser fails to launch" paths. - **Documentation:** Official documentation MUST be updated to describe Firefox support, the relevant `flutter run`/`flutter build web` flags, `flutter config` options, and platform-specific installation instructions.  ### 6. Acceptance Criteria  1. On a machine with Firefox installed, `flutter devices` lists a Firefox device. 2. `flutter run -d firefox` builds, serves, and opens the app in Firefox; editing the source triggers a successful hot reload, and the reload is reflected in the Firefox window. 3. `flutter run -d firefox` in a headless environment (e.g., Linux CI with `xvfb` or `--headless` flag) completes successfully without a display server. 4. Debugging (breakpoints, stepping, widget inspector, console logs) is functional in the Firefox target. 5. `flutter build web --target-browser firefox` (or the agreed equivalent option) completes successfully and outputs a valid Gecko-compatible build. 6. `flutter config --enable-firefox` / `--no-enable-firefox` toggles discovery as specified, and the setting is reflected in `flutter doctor`. 7. With Firefox absent, `flutter run -d firefox` fails fast with an actionable message naming the expected install locations and installation instructions for the host platform. 8. `FIREFOX_EXECUTABLE` (or the agreed override variable) pointing to a non-standard binary results in that binary being used. 9. All existing repository tests pass on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and new tests cover the Firefox-specific code paths. 10. Documentation reflects the shipped behavior.  ### 7. Risks and Considerations  - **Engine/renderer parity:** Some web features (e.g., certain canvaskit behaviors, WebGL/CanvasKit download paths, `dart:js` interop details) may behave differently in Gecko; the requirement must be validated against all supported renderers. - **DevTools protocol differences:** The debugging experience may rely on Chromium DevTools Protocol today; the implementation must confirm or provide an equivalent mechanism for Gecko before declaring FR-4 satisfied. - **Sandboxed Linux installs:** Snap/Flatpak Firefox installations may not permit arbitrary launch flags or profile directories; these cases must be detected and reported clearly rather than failing obscurely. - **Flutter SDK versioning:** Where Gecko support depends on a minimum engine/SDK version, that minimum MUST be documented and enforced with a clear error for users on older versions.

issue_title: Implement namespaces in GDScript
requirement: Add namespace support to GDScript, enabling developers to declare named scopes that group related classes, constants, enums, and other declarations. Namespace members must be accessible via qualified names (e.g., `NamespaceName.MemberName`) and must be isolated from the global scope to prevent identifier collisions between different libraries and modules, including support for nested namespaces. The feature must maintain backward compatibility with existing GDScript code that does not use namespaces.
