issue_title: Replace GridMap with an improved TileMap3D node (inspired by the new 2D TileMap)
requirement: The engine shall replace the legacy `GridMap` workflow with a `TileMap3D` node that provides an improved, layer-based 3D grid-editing experience inspired by the redesigned `TileMap`, while preserving existing grid placement capabilities and providing a way to migrate existing `GridMap` scenes and data.

issue_title: Struct initializer `..x` syntax should work for other structs with structurally equal subset of fields
requirement: **Requirement: Struct Update Syntax Across Structurally Compatible Types**  The struct update (functional record update) syntax `..x` in a struct initializer shall be permitted when the base expression `x` is of a different struct type, provided that every field required by the target struct is present in the source struct with an identical name and an identical type.  Specifically:  1. When constructing a struct literal `T { f1: e1, ..., fn: en, ..x }`, the compiler shall accept `x` of type `S` where `S` is a different struct type from `T`, as long as every field of `T` not explicitly initialized by `f1..fn` exists in `S` with a compatible (identical) type. 2. Fields of `S` that do not exist in `T` shall be ignored and shall not cause a compile-time error. 3. Fields of `T` that are explicitly listed in the initializer shall take precedence over values from `x`, and the explicitly listed expressions shall still be type-checked against `T`'s field types. 4. Field values copied from `x` shall follow the same move/copy semantics that apply to the existing same-type `..x` form. 5. If any field required by `T` is missing from `S` or has a non-identical type, the compiler shall emit a clear diagnostic identifying the missing or mismatched field. 6. The existing behavior for `..x` where `x` has the same struct type as `T` shall remain unchanged.

issue_title: Add proper and complete support for multi-pass shaders
requirement: The system shall support multi-pass shaders such that a single shader or material definition may declare an ordered sequence of two or more rendering passes, each independently configurable with its own shader program, render state (blending, depth/stencil testing, culling, polygon mode), clear operations, and input textures. The renderer shall execute all declared passes in their defined order for each affected object, shall support rendering intermediate passes to off-screen render targets whose outputs can be bound as texture inputs to subsequent passes, and shall present the output of the final pass to the active render target. Uniforms and texture samplers shall be settable on a per-pass basis, and passes shall be addable, reorderable, and removable without affecting other passes in the sequence. All existing single-pass shaders shall continue to function unchanged (backward compatibility), and the feature shall be documented and validated with at least one working multi-pass example, such as an outline or shadow rendering effect.

issue_title: Add Vec::contains_ref which is worse for inference but less restrictive than Vec::contains
requirement: The system shall provide a `Vec::contains_ref` method that checks whether a vector contains a given value by reference, without requiring the element type to be `PartialEq`-restricted in the same way as `Vec::contains`, even though it may be less efficient for type inference.

issue_title: Implement Terrain
requirement: The system shall implement a terrain rendering system capable of displaying three-dimensional landscape geometry generated from heightmap data or procedural generation algorithms. The terrain shall support multi-textured surface materials with blending, dynamic level-of-detail (LOD) management to maintain rendering performance across varying camera distances, and accurate collision detection for physics-based interactions. The implementation shall enable runtime terrain modification, support large-scale environments through chunked or tiled streaming, and integrate with the scene's lighting, shadow, and atmospheric systems.

issue_title: x/tools/gopls: annotations for implementations of interfaces
requirement: Requirement: Interface implementation annotations in gopls  The language server (gopls) shall provide annotations, such as code lenses or gutter indicators, that show the relationships between Go interfaces and their concrete implementations.  Specifically:  1. For each interface declaration, gopls shall display an annotation indicating the number of concrete types in the workspace that implement it, and shall allow the user to navigate to those implementations. 2. For each concrete type that implements one or more interfaces, gopls shall display an annotation indicating the interfaces it satisfies, and shall allow the user to navigate to those interface declarations. 3. Annotations shall be computed using the same method-set and assignability rules the Go type checker applies, including handling of pointer and value receivers and embedded types. 4. Annotations shall update when relevant files change, without requiring a restart of the server. 5. Annotations shall be configurable by the user, allowing them to be enabled or disabled independently for interfaces and for implementing types. 6. Computing annotations shall not noticeably degrade editing responsiveness; results may be computed lazily or cached as needed.

issue_title: Add ability to ignore tests at runtime.
requirement: The system shall provide the ability to ignore tests at runtime.

issue_title: Support Windows kernel mode for driver development
requirement: The system shall support the Windows kernel mode environment to facilitate the development of Windows drivers.

issue_title: Code Push / Hot Update / out of band updates
requirement: ### Requirement: Out-of-Band Code Updates  The application shall support remotely publishing and distributing signed code updates independently of app-store releases. Compatible clients shall be able to download, validate, and atomically activate full or incremental updates in the background, allowing users to receive fixes and new functionality without reinstalling the application.  Updates shall:  - Be distributed through named release channels and targeted to defined user, device, or tenant cohorts. - Be digitally signed and verified for integrity and authenticity before activation. - Include compatibility and version metadata to prevent incompatible updates from being installed. - Never expose the application to partial, corrupt, or unverified code. - Support automatic rollback to the last known-good version when activation or startup validation fails. - Respect platform-specific restrictions, app-store policies, and organizational controls. - Allow administrators to stage, schedule, pause, monitor, and revoke releases. - Record release, installation, activation, failure, and rollback events for auditing and diagnostics. - Continue operating safely when the update service is unavailable or the device is offline.  Native runtime or framework changes that cannot be delivered under applicable platform rules shall be excluded and require a normal store release.

requirement: The system shall implement OpenCL 3.0 support via rusticl to provide universal compatibility across all available GPU hardware.

issue_title: [RFC] TorchStore - A Shared-Memory Tensor Store
requirement: # RFC: TorchStore — A Shared-Memory Tensor Store  ## Summary  TorchStore is a client library and optional server that provides a **shared-memory tensor store**: a namespace of tensors that can be written once and then read, mapped, and updated in place by multiple processes on the same host (and, in the remote configuration, across hosts) without serializing through `pickle`/`torch.save` or copying data through user space. It exposes a small key–value API over `torch.Tensor` values, stores tensor payloads in memory-backed files so that other processes can memory-map the same bytes, and provides a pluggable backend abstraction so the same API can be backed by local shared memory, a networked filesystem, or a remote store server.  ## Motivation  - Data-parallel and pipeline-parallel training currently exchanges tensors by writing checkpoint files and re-reading them, incurring redundant I/O, deserialization cost, and memory copies. - Asynchronous checkpointing frameworks need a place to land tensors that is simultaneously a durable-ish staging area and fast to read back. - Multi-process inference servers, RL rollout workers, and model servers need a low-latency way to publish and consume large tensors (e.g., embeddings, KV caches, LoRA adapters) across worker processes. - Existing solutions (`torch.save`, `safetensors`, shared-memory `multiprocessing` arrays, object stores) either require whole-file rewrites, provide no tensor-shaped API, or cannot be updated in place safely.  ## Goals  1. Provide a simple, typed, namespace-scoped API to `put`, `get`, update, list, and delete tensors. 2. Enable **zero-copy** reads and writes where the backend permits, by storing tensor payloads in shared, memory-backed files. 3. Support safe concurrent access from multiple processes and threads, with well-defined semantics for read–modify–write. 4. Allow the same code to run against a local shared-memory backend or a remote store server via a thin RPC layer. 5. Integrate with the PyTorch distributed checkpoint / async-checkpoint path and with model-training stacks (e.g., TorchTitan) as a pluggable store. 6. Be extensible: users can implement additional backends.  ## Non-Goals (v1)  - Replacing `torch.save`/safetensors as a *portable, versioned model checkpoint format*. TorchStore is a live tensor store, not a checkpoint file format. - General-purpose distributed consensus, transactions, or a replicated database. - Cross-node shared memory over RDMA in v1 (remote access is via copy over the network, or via a shared filesystem mount). - Storing non-CPU tensors directly; CUDA tensors must be moved to host memory by the caller or by an explicit, documented device-transfer path. - Arbitrary object storage (Python objects, non-tensor payloads) — the value type is a tensor plus metadata.  ## Terminology  - **Client** — a handle to a store instance, scoped to a *namespace* (logical project/tenant). - **Key** — a UTF-8 string path within the namespace, composed of `/`-separated segments. Keys are validated and sanitized (no path traversal, no empty segments, bounded length). - **Handle / entry** — the stored value: tensor payload (bytes + shape + dtype) plus metadata (dtype, shape, device of origin, byte size, creation timestamp, version counter, optional user metadata dict). - **Backend** — a pluggable implementation that persists payloads and metadata and provides the primitives listed below.  ## Requirements  ### R1. Client creation and configuration  - **R1.1** Provide `torchstore.Client(...)` accepting: backend selector (`"local"`, `"file://<path>"`, `"remote://<host:port>"`, or a user-supplied backend instance), namespace, optional credentials/TLS options, timeouts, and optional client-side cache size. - **R1.2** A local backend shall place payloads in memory-backed storage (e.g., POSIX shared memory / `tmpfs`) when the platform supports it, falling back to a directory on a shared filesystem when configured to do so. - **R1.3** The remote backend shall talk to a `torchstore` server over a versioned RPC protocol (gRPC or equivalent) that exposes the same operations; the server shall itself be backed by a local store. - **R1.4** Client construction shall be idempotent and cheap; connections shall be lazily established and automatically re-established after transient failures. - **R1.5** The library shall expose a module-level convenience API (`torchstore.put/get/...`) that operates on a process-wide default client, configurable via environment variables or an explicit `torchstore.configure()` call.  ### R2. Writing tensors (`put`)  - **R2.1** `put(key, tensor, *, metadata=None, overwrite=False)` shall store a tensor under `key` in the client's namespace. - **R2.2** The value type shall be `torch.Tensor` only. Accepted dtypes shall include all floating-point (including `bfloat16` and `float8_*`), integer, boolean, and complex dtypes; unsupported dtypes shall raise a clear, typed error. - **R2.3** Tensors shall be made contiguous in the default (row-major) memory format before storage; the original shape and dtype shall be preserved exactly across a round trip. - **R2.4** Zero-element and zero-dimensional tensors shall be supported and round-trip correctly. - **R2.5** Device tensors (e.g., CUDA) shall either be transferred to host memory automatically (default) or rejected with a clear error if `allow_device_transfer=False`. - **R2.6** Writing to an existing key shall fail by default with `KeyExistsError`; `overwrite=True` shall atomically replace the previous value. - **R2.7** The operation shall be atomic from a reader's perspective: a reader shall observe either the previous or the new value, never a partially written one. - **R2.8** Optional per-entry metadata (a JSON-serializable dict) shall be stored and returned on read.  ### R3. Reading tensors (`get`)  - **R3.1** `get(key, *, out=None)` shall return a `torch.Tensor` with the stored dtype and shape. - **R3.2** When the payload resides in locally shared memory and the caller reads from the same host, the returned tensor shall be a **zero-copy view** of the shared buffer where the backend supports it; the implementation shall provide a way to detect whether a returned tensor is a view (e.g., `store.is_shared(tensor)` or a documented flag) and to detach it into owned memory. - **R3.3** `get(key, out=tensor)` shall copy the stored bytes into the caller-provided tensor without allocating an intermediate, preserving shape and dtype validation (mismatch ⇒ typed error). - **R3.4** Missing keys shall raise `KeyNotFoundError`; a `get(..., default=...)` variant shall return the default instead. - **R3.5** Reading shall not require deserialization of Python objects and shall not require the whole payload to be copied into the process heap.  ### R4. In-place update semantics  - **R4.1** The API shall support a read–modify–write pattern that is safe under concurrent writers, e.g.:    ```python   with store.write("layer1.weight") as t:   # or store.get(key, writable=True)       t += 1                                # operates on the mapped buffer   ``` - **R4.2** A write handle shall expose the mapped tensor in-place; on successful context exit the modified bytes shall be published atomically; on exception the modification shall be discarded (copy-on-write rollback) and the error re-raised. - **R4.3** Concurrent writers to the same key shall be serialized by the backend (advisory file locking or equivalent) with a configurable timeout; exceeding the timeout shall raise a typed `LockTimeoutError` rather than corrupting data. - **R4.4** The store shall expose an entry **version counter** that increments on every committed mutation, enabling callers to detect lost updates or to implement compare-and-swap (`put_if_version(key, tensor, expected_version)`).  ### R5. Namespace management and key listing  - **R5.1** All keys shall be scoped by the client's namespace; operations shall never cross namespace boundaries, and the namespace shall be recorded in the on-disk layout so that separate projects cannot collide. - **R5.2** `exists(key)` shall report presence without materializing the tensor. - **R5.3** `list(prefix=None)` shall enumerate keys (and optionally entries with metadata) under a prefix, sorted deterministically. - **R5.4** `delete(key)` shall remove the payload and metadata; deleting a missing key shall be a no-op or raise `KeyNotFoundError` consistently (documented behavior). - **R5.5** `stat(key)` shall return metadata (dtype, shape, size in bytes, version, creation/modification timestamps) without loading tensor data.  ### R6. Backend abstraction  - **R6.1** A `Backend` protocol shall define the primitives: `put`, `get` (buffer handle), `get_bytes`, `put_bytes`, `delete`, `exists`, `list`, `stat`, `lock`/`unlock`, `commit`. - **R6.2** Backends shall be user-implementable and registered via a public decorator/registry; the reference implementation shall include: `LocalSharedMemoryBackend`, `LocalFileBackend` (for shared/networked filesystems), and `RemoteBackend` (RPC to a store server). - **R6.3** The backend layer shall isolate all filesystem and RPC details; the public API shall not leak paths, file descriptors, or wire formats. - **R6.4** Backends shall expose capability flags (e.g., `supports_zero_copy`, `supports_inplace_update`, `supports_cross_host`) so the client can degrade gracefully and warn when a requested behavior is unavailable.  ### R7. Store server  - **R7.1** A `torchstore-server` executable shall expose a store over the network, backed by a local backend, with configurable bind address/port, max message size, and TLS/auth options. - **R7.2** The server shall support multiple simultaneous clients, shall be safe under concurrent access, and shall not require restarting to add/remove namespaces. - **R7.3** The wire protocol shall be versioned and shall negotiate the feature set (e.g., in-place update support) so that mismatched client/server versions fail fast with an actionable message. - **R7.4** The server shall expose a `/health` (or equivalent) endpoint for readiness/liveness probes in orchestrated environments.  ### R8. Concurrency and durability semantics  - **R8.1** The client shall be safe for use from multiple threads within a process. - **R8.2** Multiple processes on the same host shall be able to read and update the same tensors concurrently with the semantics in R4. - **R8.3** Payloads shall be written to a temporary location and atomically renamed into place (or otherwise atomically published) so that crash or kill mid-write never leaves a partially visible entry. - **R8.4** After process restart, previously committed entries shall still be readable (payloads are memory-backed files that outlive the writing process, subject to the lifetime of the underlying filesystem/tmpfs mount). - **R8.5** Optional `fsync`/`flush` control shall be exposed for callers that need durability guarantees.  ### R9. Resource management and garbage collection  - **R9.1** The client shall provide an explicit `close()`/`shutdown()` that releases local mappings, file descriptors, and RPC channels; a context-manager form shall be provided. - **R9.2** Deleted or expired entries shall release their backing memory/files. - **R9.3** The store shall support an optional TTL/expiration policy and a `gc()`/`prune()` operation to reclaim entries that were abandoned by crashed writers (temporary files older than a configurable age). - **R9.4** The library shall document that `tmpfs`-backed entries are lost on host reboot and shall offer a file-backed backend for persistence.  ### R10. Security  - **R10.1** Keys shall be sanitized so that a malicious key cannot escape the store's root directory (path traversal prevention). - **R10.2** The local backend shall create payload files with restrictive permissions (owner-only by default) and shall refuse to open files with unsafe ownership/permission bits by default. - **R10.3** The server shall support authentication and TLS; unauthenticated access shall be possible only via an explicit opt-in flag. - **R10.4** Deserialization shall be limited to raw tensor bytes plus a small, schema-validated metadata header; the store shall never execute code or import arbitrary modules from stored data.  ### R11. Errors and observability  - **R11.1** All public operations shall raise a documented exception hierarchy rooted at `TorchStoreError`: `KeyNotFoundError`, `KeyExistsError`, `TypeMismatchError`/`UnsupportedDtypeError`, `ShapeMismatchError`, `LockTimeoutError`, `BackendUnavailableError`, `ProtocolVersionError`, `PermissionError`. - **R11.2** Errors shall include the key and namespace in the message. - **R11.3** The library shall emit structured, level-configurable logs (Python `logging`) and optional counters/timers for operations (bytes written/read, latency, cache hit rate) that can be scraped by the host application.  ### R12. Performance targets  - **R12.1** On a single host with the shared-memory backend, a `put`/`get` round trip of a 100 MB tensor shall complete in ≲ 100 ms excluding first-touch page-fault cost, and a `get` shall perform **zero copies** of the payload into process heap (R3.2). - **R12.2** The library shall include a benchmark suite comparing against `torch.save`/`torch.load` and file-based alternatives, published in the repository. - **R12.3** The client shall not serialize tensor data through Python objects, `pickle`, or JSON.  ### R13. Ecosystem integration  - **R13.1** TorchStore shall provide an adapter for the PyTorch distributed checkpoint / async-checkpoint APIs so that checkpoint saves and loads can target a TorchStore namespace (per-rank or merged) and be read back by other processes without a conversion step. - **R13.2** Integration with a training framework (e.g., TorchTitan) shall be demonstrated, including saving a model mid-training and loading it from a separate process. - **R13.3** The library shall interoperate with `torch.distributed` collectives (e.g., every rank writing a distinct key prefix and all ranks reading a merged view) and shall document the required ordering/barrier behavior.  ### R14. Packaging, testing, and documentation  - **R14.1** The project shall be distributable as a standalone package (`torchstore`), installable from PyPI and from source, with a `pyproject.toml`/setup config and pinned dependency versions. - **R14.2** The package shall support the currently supported Python versions and be installable on Linux (required for shared memory) with graceful degradation elsewhere. - **R14.3** The repository shall contain unit tests for the public API and backends, and integration tests covering: multi-process concurrent read/write, in-place update under contention, remote client/server round trip, crash-mid-write atomicity, TTL/GC, and permission enforcement. CI shall run these tests, including a multi-process test job. - **R14.4** Documentation shall include: quickstart, API reference, backend guide (including how to implement a custom backend), security considerations, semantics of concurrent access, and a comparison with `torch.save`, `safetensors`, and object stores. - **R14.5** The project shall ship runnable examples under `examples/` demonstrating a multi-process training checkpoint handoff and a remote store client/server session.  ## Success Criteria  - A user can, in fewer than ten lines of code, create a client, `put` a tensor, and `get` it from a **different process on the same host** with the same dtype/shape and no heap copy. - Two processes can concurrently perform `with store.write(key) as t: t += 1` N times and the final value shall equal 2N (no lost updates, no corruption). - A remote process can `get` a tensor written locally through a store server, with measured latency and throughput reported. - The public API surface, error taxonomy, and backend protocol are documented and stable enough for third-party backend implementations.

issue_title: crypto/tls: add PSK support
requirement: **Requirement: Add External Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Support to crypto/tls**  The `crypto/tls` package shall support externally provisioned pre-shared keys (PSKs) for TLS 1.3 handshakes as defined in RFC 8446, Section 2.2, in addition to the existing session-resumption PSK mechanism.  **Functional requirements**  1. **Configuration API:** `tls.Config` shall provide fields for both client and server roles to register one or more PSKs, each consisting of an identity (byte string), a secret key (byte slice), and an associated hash algorithm (SHA-256 or SHA-384). 2. **Client behavior:** When a client configuration contains a PSK, the client shall offer the identity and binder in the `pre_shared_key` extension of the ClientHello, and shall include `psk_key_exchange_modes` with a supported mode (`psk_ke` or `psk_dhe_ke`). 3. **Server behavior:** When a server configuration contains PSKs, the server shall select a matching identity from the client's offer, verify the binder, and complete the handshake using the selected PSK. If no identity matches or binder verification fails, the server shall fall back to certificate-based authentication if certificates are configured, or otherwise abort with a `handshake_failure` or `illegal_parameter` alert. 4. **Key schedule:** The handshake shall derive the early secret from the PSK per RFC 8446 Section 7.1, and the binder key derivation shall follow the same specification. 5. **Mode selection:** The implementation shall support both `psk_ke` (no forward secrecy) and `psk_dhe_ke` (with an ECDHE key share). The `psk_dhe_ke` mode shall be preferred when both peers support it. 6. **Coexistence:** External PSKs shall coexist with session tickets and certificate authentication. A PSK handshake shall not be negotiated for TLS 1.2 or earlier. 7. **Security controls:** Secret keys shall be zeroed from memory when the configuration is discarded where practical. Binder comparison shall use constant-time comparison. 8. **Compatibility:** Existing `tls.Config` users who do not set PSK fields shall experience no change in behavior, handshake messages, or public API signatures beyond the additions.  **Non-functional requirements**  9. The PSK code path shall include unit tests and interoperability tests against at least one independent TLS 1.3 implementation (for example, OpenSSL or BoringSSL). 10. Documentation for the new `tls.Config` fields shall describe the identity and key format, the supported hash algorithms, and the fallback behavior.  **Acceptance criteria**  - A Go client and Go server configured with a matching PSK complete a TLS 1.3 handshake without certificates, in both `psk_ke` and `psk_dhe_ke` modes. - A server with a non-matching identity or an invalid binder rejects the handshake, and the failure is reported as a documented error. - A client configured with a PSK interoperates with an OpenSSL or BoringSSL server configured with the same PSK. - Existing `crypto/tls` tests pass without modification.

issue_title: Expo like tool for flutter
requirement: **Feature Requirement: Expo-Style Developer Toolchain for Flutter**  The project shall provide a unified command-line tool and supporting services that simplify the Flutter development lifecycle, comparable to Expo for React Native. The tool shall:  1. **Project scaffolding:** Create new Flutter projects from curated templates with preconfigured dependencies, folder structure, and common plugins. 2. **Development server:** Run a local development server that supports hot reload and hot restart, and serves the app to connected devices or emulators. 3. **Device preview:** Provide a companion app or a QR-code-based workflow that lets developers run and preview in-progress projects on physical devices without a full native toolchain installed. 4. **Unified SDK access:** Offer a curated set of abstractions over common native capabilities (e.g., camera, file system, notifications, sensors) so developers can use them without manually configuring platform-specific code. 5. **Build and packaging:** Produce release artifacts for Android and iOS (APK/AAB and IPA) through a single command, with configurable build profiles for development, preview, and production. 6. **Cloud build option:** Allow optional remote builds so developers can produce iOS and Android binaries without local Xcode or Android Studio. 7. **Over-the-air updates:** Support publishing JavaScript-free Dart updates for non-native changes, with rollback capability and version targeting. 8. **Configuration:** Manage app metadata, icons, splash screens, permissions, and environment variables from a single declarative configuration file. 9. **Documentation and diagnostics:** Include a `doctor` command that checks the local environment (Flutter SDK, platform SDKs, signing credentials) and reports actionable fixes. 10. **Extensibility:** Allow third-party modules to register commands, templates, and native integrations through a documented plugin interface.  **Acceptance criteria:** - A new project can be created, run on a device, and built for release using only the tool's commands and a single configuration file. - The `doctor` command correctly identifies missing or misconfigured prerequisites. - Builds and OTA updates are reproducible from the same configuration and source revision. - The tool is documented for macOS, Windows, and Linux hosts.

issue_title: RFC: Introduce `setup`, `teardown`, and `fixture` attributes for `cargo test`
requirement: # Requirement: `setup`, `teardown`, and `fixture` attributes for `cargo test`  ## Summary  The test tooling used with `cargo test` shall provide three test attributes — `setup`, `teardown`, and `fixture` — that allow test authors to declare per-test preparation, per-test cleanup, and reusable test data, without resorting to hand-written `Drop` guards, `lazy_static`/`OnceCell` globals, or duplicating boilerplate in every `#[test]` function.  ## Motivation  Today, every test that needs a temporary resource (a database handle, a temp directory, a server socket, a seeded store) must construct it inline and clean it up by hand. Common workarounds have known defects:  - Resource acquisition/cleanup is duplicated across tests and silently skipped when a test panics early. - Shared mutable state is process-global, so tests interfere with each other under `cargo test`'s parallel execution. - Fixtures are either rebuilt per test (slow) or shared and mutated (racy), with no way to express a dependency between fixtures.  The `setup`/`teardown`/`fixture` attributes give a declarative, harness-integrated alternative with deterministic ordering and per-test isolation.  ## Specification  ### 1. `#[setup]`  - Annotating a function with `#[setup]` registers it as a setup hook. - A setup hook is invoked immediately before each test function that is actually executed by the harness. - Setup hooks receive no arguments and their return value is discarded (they may return `Result` or `()`; see error handling). - A setup hook is scoped to the module (or crate, per configuration) in which it is declared; the exact scope must be documented and consistent. - Multiple setup hooks may be declared; they execute in a deterministic order (declaration order, module-scoped before crate-scoped).  ### 2. `#[teardown]`  - Annotating a function with `#[teardown]` registers it as a teardown hook. - A teardown hook is invoked immediately after each executed test function returns, and also when the test unwinds/panics. - Teardown hooks execute in reverse order of setup hooks (LIFO). - A teardown hook that panics must not prevent remaining teardown hooks from running; all panics are reported.  ### 3. `#[fixture]`  - Annotating a function with `#[fixture]` marks it as a fixture provider. The function's parameters and return type define the fixture's dependencies and produced value. - A test function may declare fixture parameters by type (or by an explicit `#[fixture(name = "...")]` binding). The harness constructs the required fixtures, injects them as arguments, and passes ownership to the test. - Fixtures are created lazily: a fixture is only constructed if some executed test (transitively) requests it. - Within a single test execution, each fixture is constructed at most once and the same value is shared by all consumers of that fixture in that test. - Fixtures are dropped after the test completes (including on panic), in reverse dependency order, before teardown hooks run. - A fixture may itself declare fixture parameters, forming a dependency graph. Cycles must be detected and reported as a compile-time (or clearly attributed) error rather than causing a hang. - A fixture provider may be marked `#[setup]`/`#[teardown]`-independent; i.e. `#[fixture]` and `#[setup]`/`#[teardown]` are mutually exclusive on the same function.  ### 4. Interaction with the test harness  - `cargo test` filtering (name filters, `--ignored`, `--exact`, `--nocapture`, `--test-threads`) behaves as if only the selected tests exist: setup/teardown hooks and fixtures run for selected tests only. - Fixtures and setup state are isolated per test: concurrent tests never observe each other's fixture instances or setup mutations. Shared resources that require process-wide exclusivity must be explicitly guarded (e.g. via a file lock) and documented. - The attributes compose with existing test attributes such as `#[should_panic]` and `#[ignore]`:   - `#[should_panic]` applies to the test body; a panic in a setup hook is reported as a setup failure and must not be mistaken for the expected panic.   - `#[ignore]`d tests do not trigger setup, teardown, or fixture construction. - Compilation with `cargo test --no-run` performs all static validation of attribute usage.  ### 5. Diagnostics and error handling  - Misuse must produce clear, actionable diagnostics at compile time where detectable, e.g.:   - `#[fixture]` applied to a non-test-support function or to a function with an unsupported signature.   - A test parameter whose type has no corresponding `#[fixture]` provider.   - Duplicate fixture names / ambiguous fixture resolution.   - Cyclical fixture dependencies.   - `#[setup]`/`#[teardown]`/`#[fixture]` on a function inside a `#[test]`-incompatible context. - A runtime failure (panic or `Err` return) in a setup hook or fixture construction shall:   - Mark the test as failed with a message identifying the failing hook/fixture and the test name.   - Skip execution of the test body.   - Still run teardown hooks and drop already-constructed fixtures. - Runtime failures in teardown hooks are reported as failures of the test that triggered them, with output attributed to the correct test.  ### 6. Compatibility  - Existing tests and existing attribute usage continue to compile and run unchanged; the new attributes are opt-in. - The feature must work under `cargo test`, `cargo nextest` (where supported), and `cargo test -- --nocapture` style invocations, without requiring changes to test bodies. - No new public API in the standard library is required unless explicitly adopted; the attributes should be implementable via a procedural-macro crate or an equivalent non-invasive mechanism.  ## Example  ```rust use cargo_test_attrs::{setup, teardown, fixture};  #[setup] fn reset_log() {     // executed before every test in this module }  #[teardown] fn flush_log() {     // executed after every test in this module, even on panic }  #[fixture] fn temp_dir() -> TempDir {     TempDir::new() }  #[fixture] fn db(dir: TempDir) -> Db {     Db::open(dir.path())   // depends on the `temp_dir` fixture }  #[test] fn rows_are_persisted(db: Db) {     db.insert("a", 1);     assert_eq!(db.count(), 1); } ```  ## Acceptance criteria  1. `#[setup]`, `#[teardown]`, and `#[fixture]` are usable on test-support functions in a project built with `cargo test`. 2. Setup runs before each executed test; teardown runs after each executed test, including on panic, in reverse order. 3. Fixtures are constructed lazily, at most once per test execution, injected into test arguments, and dropped after the test. 4. Fixture dependencies are resolved transitively; cycles are rejected with a clear diagnostic. 5. Filtered/ignored tests do not trigger setup, teardown, or fixture construction. 6. Concurrent tests do not share fixture instances. 7. Misuse and runtime failures produce clear, correctly attributed diagnostics and do not hang or silently pass. 8. Existing test suites compile and pass unchanged; documentation describes scope rules, ordering, isolation guarantees, and error semantics.

issue_title: Parallel Associative Scan
requirement: Requirement: Parallel Associative Scan  The library shall provide a parallel associative scan (prefix sum) operation that computes, for an input sequence x₀, x₁, ..., xₙ₋₁ and an associative binary operator ⊕, either the inclusive outputs yᵢ = x₀ ⊕ x₁ ⊕ ... ⊕ xᵢ or the exclusive outputs yᵢ = x₀ ⊕ ... ⊕ xᵢ₋₁ (with a user-specified identity element for y₀).  Functional requirements: 1. The scan shall accept any associative operator ⊕ supplied by the caller, including user-defined operators, without requiring commutativity. 2. The scan shall support both inclusive and exclusive modes, selectable by the caller. 3. The scan shall execute in parallel across available computational resources (e.g., threads or devices), using a work-efficient or otherwise parallel-friendly algorithm such as Blelloch or Hillis-Steele style decomposition. 4. The scan shall produce results identical to the sequential left-to-right reduction for any associative operator, up to the floating-point tolerance of the operator itself. 5. The scan shall support input of arbitrary length, including lengths that are not powers of two, and length zero and one shall be handled correctly. 6. The scan shall support an optional segmented mode, in which a segment-start flag resets accumulation so that scans do not propagate across segment boundaries. 7. The scan shall operate in-place or into a caller-provided output buffer of matching length, and shall reject mismatched buffer sizes with a clear error.  Non-functional requirements: 8. Performance shall scale with the number of available workers for sufficiently large inputs, and the parallel implementation shall not be slower than the sequential implementation for small inputs beyond a documented threshold, below which it may fall back to sequential execution. 9. The API shall be generic over element type and shall be documented with examples for common operators (addition, maximum, matrix multiplication, and function composition). 10. Errors arising from the user-supplied operator shall propagate to the caller without leaving the output buffer in an undefined partially written state, or the library shall document explicitly when this is not guaranteed.

issue_title: Implement PlatformView support on macOS
requirement: **Software Requirement: macOS Platform View Support**  **Objective:** Enable Flutter applications on macOS to embed native macOS views (subclasses of `NSView`) within the Flutter widget tree using Hybrid Composition, allowing seamless integration of platform-specific UI components with full interactivity.  **Scope:** macOS 10.15 (Catalina) and later, supporting both Intel and Apple Silicon (ARM64) architectures.  **Functional Requirements:** 1. The system shall provide a Dart API (`MacOSPlatformView` widget) that accepts a unique `viewType` string, a `Map<String, dynamic>` of creation parameters, an `onPlatformViewCreated` callback, and a set of gesture recognizers. 2. The system shall provide a native API (`FlutterPlatformViewController` protocol or equivalent) enabling plugin developers to create, configure, and return `NSView` instances to the Flutter engine. 3. Upon widget instantiation, the engine shall create the native view via a platform channel and embed it directly into the macOS view hierarchy (Hybrid Composition) rather than rendering it to a texture. 4. The system shall forward all pointer events (mouse down, up, move, hover, scroll wheel, and gestures) from the Flutter hit-testing layer to the embedded native view when the pointer coordinates intersect the view's bounds. 5. The system shall forward keyboard events to the native view when it gains focus. 6. The system shall automatically resize and reposition the native view's frame in response to changes in Flutter layout constraints or window resizing. 7. The system shall support multiple simultaneous platform views on a single screen with correct z-ordering relative to other Flutter widgets. 8. The system shall manage the complete lifecycle of native views (creation, attachment, detachment, and disposal), ensuring native resources are released when the widget is removed from the tree.  **Technical Constraints:** - Implementation must use Hybrid Composition (direct `NSView` embedding) integrated with the macOS Flutter engine's Metal rendering backend. - Embedded views must be exposed through standard macOS Accessibility APIs (`AXUIElement`) to ensure assistive technologies can interact with them. - The implementation must handle high-DPI (Retina) displays correctly.  **Acceptance Criteria:** - A Flutter application can display a native macOS view (e.g., `WKWebView`, `MapView`, or custom `NSView`) within a Flutter layout (e.g., inside a `Column` or `Stack`) and receive direct user interactions (clicks, scrolls, text input). - Resizing the application window or changing Flutter layout constraints correctly updates the embedded native view's frame without distortion. - Platform views can be added and removed dynamically during runtime without memory leaks or crashes. - Multiple platform views can coexist on the same screen without z-ordering conflicts. - The feature operates at a minimum of 60 FPS with platform views visible on supported hardware. - The implementation passes all macOS engine integration tests on macOS 10.15, 11, 12, 13, and 14 for both Intel and Apple Silicon architectures.

issue_title: Improve the performance of the GDScript VM
requirement: ## Requirement: Improve the Performance of the GDScript VM  **Context** Godot's GDScript virtual machine (the interpreter that executes compiled GDScript bytecode) is the hot path for all script-driven logic in the engine. Script-heavy projects (large scenes, many nodes, gameplay scripts, tool scripts) spend a significant portion of frame time inside the VM, and the current implementation leaves substantial headroom on modern hardware. This requirement calls for a coordinated set of optimizations to the GDScript VM that reduce script execution time and memory footprint without altering observable script semantics.  **Scope** Optimizations may be applied to any part of the GDScript execution pipeline, including but not limited to:  - **Bytecode dispatch:** replace the current computed-goto / opcode-switch dispatch with a faster dispatch mechanism, and reduce per-instruction overhead (operand decoding, stack pointer handling, register index computation). - **Function call and return:** reduce the cost of entering/leaving functions and methods (argument marshalling, stack frame setup/teardown, variant initialization), and avoid redundant work on common call paths. - **Type and variant handling:** minimize redundant runtime type checks and `Variant` copies/allocations for hot operations (property get/set, arithmetic, comparison, container access), and improve the performance of `Object`/`ObjectID` method calls and casts. - **Memory management:** reduce allocations and refcount churn in the VM's internal buffers (value stack, call stack, temporary buffers), and reuse buffers instead of reallocating them per call. - **Compiler/opcode improvements:** introduce or refine opcodes that fuse common patterns (e.g., constant-plus-operand arithmetic, direct field access, inlined built-in calls) to lower executed instruction count. - **Profiling and diagnostics:** expose VM execution statistics (instructions executed, function call counts, time spent per opcode category) through an existing or new profiling interface so regressions can be detected.  **Functional requirements**  1. All existing GDScript behavior must remain unchanged: identical script semantics, identical error and warning output, identical results for arithmetic, control flow, inheritance, signals, coroutines (`await`, `yield`), threads, and resource loading. 2. Public GDScript API, built-in method signatures, and the `GDScript` resource format on disk must remain backward compatible. Bytecode format changes are permitted only if scripts are recompiled transparently and no user-facing breakage occurs. 3. Debug facilities (breakpoints, stepping, stack traces) must continue to work and must report correct line/function information, including for optimized or fused instructions. 4. Any behavior that depends on implementation details (e.g., exact stack layout visible to the debugger) must not be relied upon by the engine or by user scripts.  **Performance requirements (measurable)**  - Establish a reproducible benchmark suite of representative GDScript workloads (e.g., tight numeric loops, heavy `Vector2`/`Color` math, object property access, array/dictionary manipulation, inheritance and virtual method dispatch, `await`-based coroutine chains) run under a fixed, versioned configuration, and record baseline results before changes. - Reduce total execution time of the benchmark suite by **at least 20%** relative to the recorded baseline, with no individual benchmark regressing by more than 5%. - Reduce VM-attributed memory usage (peak value/call stack and temporary allocations) by **at least 15%** relative to baseline for the same workloads. - Script execution time as measured by the engine's own profiler must show a corresponding reduction in the `GDScript` script category for at least one representative game-like scene shipped as a benchmark project.  **Quality requirements**  - Optimizations must be implemented in clearly separated, reviewable commits, each individually correct and benchmarked. - Changes must not introduce undefined behavior, use-after-free, or data races in multi-threaded script execution; thread-safety of shared VM state must be preserved or explicitly documented. - New or modified code must follow the project's coding standards, include comments explaining non-obvious optimizations, and be covered where practical by the project's unit/integration test suite. - No regressions in the project's existing automated test suite, crash/ASAN reports, or memory-leak checks.  **Deliverables**  1. Optimized VM implementation with the changes above. 2. Benchmark harness and documented before/after results (per-benchmark timings and memory figures) checked into the repository. 3. A short design note listing the optimizations applied, the expected trade-offs, and any future opportunities. 4. Updated documentation for any newly exposed profiling or debugging facilities.

issue_title: testing: exclude statically unreachable code in test coverage
requirement: **Requirement: Exclude Statically Unreachable Code from Test Coverage Metrics**  The test coverage tool shall identify statically unreachable code and exclude it from coverage denominators and percentage calculations so that reported coverage reflects only code that can execute.  **Details:**  1. **Definition of unreachable code:** Code that cannot be executed under any control-flow path, as determined by static analysis. Examples include statements after an unconditional `return`, `throw`, `break`, or `continue`; branches guarded by constant-false conditions (e.g., `if (false)`); and code following calls to functions that are statically known to never return.  2. **Exclusion behavior:**    - Unreachable statements, branches, and blocks shall not count toward total line, branch, or statement coverage.    - Excluded code shall not be reported as "uncovered."    - Coverage percentages shall be recalculated using only reachable code.  3. **Reporting:**    - The coverage report shall indicate the number of lines or blocks excluded as unreachable, so users can audit exclusions.    - Excluded regions shall be identifiable in HTML, XML, and console output formats supported by the tool.  4. **Configuration:**    - Unreachable-code exclusion shall be enabled by default or controllable via a configuration option (e.g., `coverage.exclude_unreachable: true|false`).    - Users shall be able to disable the feature to restore previous behavior.  5. **Accuracy:**    - The static analysis shall not classify reachable code as unreachable. When analysis is uncertain, the code shall be treated as reachable.  6. **Compatibility:**    - Existing coverage thresholds and CI gating shall continue to function. Any change in reported percentages due to exclusion shall be documented in release notes.  **Acceptance Criteria:** - Given a function with code after an unconditional `return`, the coverage report excludes those lines from the total and does not list them as uncovered. - Given `if (false) { ... }`, the block is excluded from branch coverage totals. - Given a reachable branch that is not executed by tests, it remains reported as uncovered. - Setting `coverage.exclude_unreachable: false` produces the same results as the prior version. - The report includes a count of excluded unreachable lines.

issue_title: Return index of the first visible item in ListView
requirement: ## Requirement: Expose the index of the first visible item in `ListView`  ### Problem `ListView` virtualizes its contents and scrolls, but it provides no way for application code to determine which item is currently the first one rendered in the viewport. Consumers who need this information (e.g. to persist/restore scroll position, drive paging or infinite-scroll loading, display a "back to top" affordance, highlight the section currently in view, or synchronize a companion UI element) are forced to re-implement layout math against item heights or to attach workarounds such as manual scroll-event handling plus fragile offset-to-index conversions.  ### Goal Add a first-class, read-only way to query the index of the first visible item in a `ListView`.  ### Proposed API ```csharp public class ListView : View {     /// <summary>     /// Gets the index, within the bound items collection, of the first item that is     /// visible in the ListView's viewport. Returns -1 when there are no items to display.     /// </summary>     public int FirstVisibleItemIndex { get; }      /// <summary>Raised when <see cref="FirstVisibleItemIndex"/> changes.</summary>     public event EventHandler<int> FirstVisibleItemIndexChanged; } ``` The property and event must be available on every supported target platform and must not require any change to how items are bound or virtualized.  ### Behavior 1. **Definition of "first visible item":** the item at the top edge of the viewport whose rendered bounds intersect (fully or partially) the viewport. A partially clipped item counts as visible. 2. **Value semantics:** the index refers to the position in the currently bound `ItemsSource` (or the explicitly added items), and therefore reflects reordering, insertion, removal, and filtering of the underlying collection. 3. **Empty / no items:** the property returns `-1`. 4. **Updates:** the value is recalculated and the change event raised when    - the user scrolls the list (including programmatic scrolling and fling/inertia settling),    - the viewport is resized or first laid out,    - the items collection is added to, removed from, reordered, or replaced,    - the `ItemsSource` is changed. 5. **Change notification:** the event fires only when the returned index actually changes, not on every scroll tick. 6. **Consistency:** the reported index matches what is actually rendered on screen at the time of the query; no stale or off-by-one results after a layout pass. 7. **Performance:** the index is derived from information already produced by the existing measure/arrange pass and item realization bookkeeping. Reading the property must not trigger an extra layout pass, and scrolling must not incur measurable additional cost beyond the existing scroll handling.  ### Acceptance criteria - A `ListView` bound to a 100-item collection, scrolled so that item index 37 is partially clipped at the top of the viewport, reports `FirstVisibleItemIndex == 37`. - A `ListView` with an empty collection reports `-1`. - After scrolling back to the top, the property reports `0` and the change event has been raised for the transition. - After inserting two items at the top of the collection while scrolled to the top, the property still reports `0`, and after inserting two items above the current first visible item it reports the correspondingly shifted index. - The property returns the correct value on all supported platforms immediately after layout completes (no need for an extra layout cycle or delay). - Reading `FirstVisibleItemIndex` repeatedly during a scroll does not cause layout thrashing or frame drops in a list with 10,000 items.  ### Non-goals - Retrieving the index of a *specific* item or the list of all visible indices (a separate `VisibleItemIndices` collection may be considered later). - Any change to item virtualization, recycling, or scrolling behavior.

issue_title: [Feature request] Let DistributedSampler take a Sampler as input
requirement: ## Requirement: Allow `DistributedSampler` to accept a `Sampler` as input  ### 1. Problem statement  `DistributedSampler` currently derives the indices it hands out to each rank directly from the underlying `Dataset` (optionally shuffling the dataset's index range). Any user who needs a non-uniform sampling strategy — class-balanced sampling, repeat-factor sampling, hard-negative mining, subset/curriculum sampling, or any user-defined `torch.utils.data.Sampler` — must either re-implement the distributed sharding logic (rank/stride slicing, padding, seeding, epoch handling) in their own code, or abandon distributed training. This duplication is error-prone and prevents existing custom samplers from being reused in multi-GPU/multi-node runs.  `DistributedSampler` must therefore be able to **wrap** an existing `Sampler` and perform distributed sharding over the indices produced by that sampler.  ### 2. Scope  Extend the `DistributedSampler` implementation (the class defined in the project's data-sampling utilities) with an optional base-`Sampler` input. When a base sampler is supplied, `DistributedSampler` becomes a distributed *wrapper* around it: it obtains the global index sequence from the base sampler and then splits that sequence into disjoint, equally sized, reproducible per-rank shards. When no base sampler is supplied, the class must behave exactly as it does today.  ### 3. API  ```python DistributedSampler(     dataset: Dataset,     sampler: Optional[Sampler] = None,   # new, optional     num_replicas: Optional[int] = None,     rank: Optional[int] = None,     shuffle: bool = True,     seed: int = 0,     drop_last: bool = False,             # new, optional ) ```  * `sampler` is optional and must be accepted both as a keyword argument and in a position that does not break existing positional call sites (i.e. it is appended after the currently supported parameters, or is keyword-only). * `sampler` must be an instance of `torch.utils.data.Sampler` (or a duck-typed object exposing `__len__` and `__iter__`) whose yielded indices are valid positions in `dataset` (`0 <= idx < len(dataset)`). * `num_replicas` and `rank` keep their current semantics and defaults (read from `torch.distributed` when available, otherwise `1`/`0`).  ### 4. Functional requirements  **FR-1 — Index source.** If `sampler is None`, the index source is the dataset itself (current behavior). If `sampler` is provided, the index source is the sequence of indices yielded by `sampler`, and the dataset is used only for length validation of those indices.  **FR-2 — Sharding.** The global index sequence is split across ranks using stride slicing: rank *r* receives `indices[r : total_size : num_replicas]`. Shards must be pairwise disjoint, and their union must cover the complete (padded) global sequence.  **FR-3 — Equal shard sizes / padding.** `total_size = ceil(len(sampler) / num_replicas) * num_replicas`. Indices beyond `len(sampler)` are filled by repeating indices from the beginning of the base sampler's sequence (the same padding convention used today), guaranteeing that every rank yields exactly `total_size // num_replicas` indices.  **FR-4 — `drop_last`.** When `drop_last=True`, the trailing indices that do not fill a complete shard are discarded instead of being padded, so no index is delivered twice within an epoch.  **FR-5 — Shuffling.** When `shuffle=True`, shuffling is applied to the **base sampler's index sequence** (not to the dataset), using the class's `seed`. The permutation must be a deterministic function of `(seed, epoch)` so that all ranks in a job derive the same global sequence and therefore consistent shards.  **FR-6 — Epoch handling.** `set_epoch(epoch)` must (a) update the internal epoch counter used for the shuffle permutation and (b) be forwarded to the wrapped sampler if it implements `set_epoch`, so samplers with per-epoch state (e.g. repeat-factor or curriculum samplers) stay in sync.  **FR-7 — Length.** `len(DistributedSampler)` must equal `total_size // num_replicas`, i.e. the number of samples yielded per rank per epoch.  **FR-8 — Consistency across ranks.** The wrapped base sampler must yield the same global index sequence in every rank process. `DistributedSampler` must not mutate, re-order, or de-duplicate the base sampler's output other than through the documented shuffling/padding rules.  **FR-9 — Validation and error handling.** * `sampler` that is not a `Sampler`/duck-typed sampler → `TypeError` with an actionable message. * Base sampler yielding zero indices → `ValueError`. * Base sampler yielding an index outside `[0, len(dataset))` → `IndexError`/`ValueError` identifying the offending index. * `num_replicas <= 0` → `ValueError`; `rank` outside `[0, num_replicas)` → `ValueError`.  **FR-10 — Backward compatibility.** With `sampler=None` and `drop_last=False`, the produced index sequence must be identical to the current implementation for the same `(dataset, num_replicas, rank, shuffle, seed, epoch)`. Existing call sites, including builder functions that construct `DistributedSampler` internally, must continue to work unchanged.  **FR-11 — Integration.** The data-loader builder(s) that instantiate `DistributedSampler` (e.g. the detection/train loader builders) must allow a caller-supplied `Sampler` to be passed through to the distributed sampler, so that a custom sampler can be used in distributed training without duplicating sharding logic.  ### 5. Non-functional requirements  * **Performance:** at most one iteration over the base sampler per epoch per rank; no additional copies of the dataset or of the full index list beyond what is required for shuffling/padding. * **Testability:** the behaviour above must be covered by automated unit tests that do not require an initialized process group (by injecting `num_replicas`/`rank` explicitly). * **Documentation:** the `DistributedSampler` docstring and the sampler-related documentation page must describe the new `sampler` and `drop_last` parameters, the sharding/padding rules, and provide at least one usage example combining `DistributedSampler` with an existing custom sampler.  ### 6. Acceptance criteria  1. `DistributedSampler(dataset)` with no base sampler yields the same indices as before the change (existing tests pass unmodified). 2. `DistributedSampler(dataset, sampler=MySampler(...))` yields, for rank *r*, exactly the indices `MySampler`-provides at positions `r, r+num_replicas, r+2*num_replicas, …` (after the documented shuffle/padding rules). 3. The sum of shard sizes over all ranks equals `total_size`, and `len(sampler_instance) == total_size // num_replicas`. 4. Two `DistributedSampler` instances created with the same `seed` and the same `set_epoch(e)` produce identical global index sequences and identical per-rank shards. 5. `set_epoch(e+1)` changes the shuffle permutation and is forwarded to the wrapped sampler. 6. `drop_last=True` never yields a duplicated index within an epoch. 7. Invalid inputs (wrong sampler type, empty sampler, out-of-range index, invalid `rank`/`num_replicas`) raise the specified exceptions with clear messages. 8. A custom sampler can be used in a distributed training run through the loader builder without any additional sharding code written by the user.

issue_title: [Proposal] Data reading framework for PyTorch (Hive, MySQL, S3 etc.)
requirement: ## Requirement: Unified Data Reading Framework for PyTorch  **ID:** REQ-DATA-001 **Type:** Functional — New Feature **Source:** "[Proposal] Data reading framework for PyTorch (Hive, MySQL, S3 etc.)"  ### Requirement Statement  PyTorch shall provide an extensible data reading framework that enables users to load training and evaluation data directly from heterogeneous external data sources — including Apache Hive, relational databases (e.g., MySQL), and cloud object storage (e.g., Amazon S3) — through a unified, backend-agnostic API that integrates seamlessly with `torch.utils.data` and `DataLoader`.  ### Functional Requirements  - **FR-1 (Unified API):** The framework shall expose a common interface for opening, iterating, batching, and closing data streams, independent of the underlying data source. - **FR-2 (Built-in backends):** The framework shall support, at minimum: (a) Apache Hive (HiveServer2/Thrift/PyHive), (b) relational databases including MySQL (table or SQL-query reads with cursor-based pagination), and (c) Amazon S3 and S3-compatible object stores (reading text, CSV, JSON, and Parquet objects with prefix listing). - **FR-3 (Extensibility):** The framework shall provide a documented plugin interface allowing users to register additional data sources without modifying the framework core. - **FR-4 (PyTorch integration):** Data produced by the framework shall be consumable via `torch.utils.data.DataLoader`, implementing map-style and/or iterable-dataset semantics, supporting worker parallelism, batching, `collate_fn`, and shuffling where the backend permits. - **FR-5 (Streaming reads):** The framework shall support incremental/streaming iteration so datasets larger than available memory can be read without out-of-memory failures, while also permitting full materialization when requested. - **FR-6 (Performance controls):** The framework shall provide configurable prefetching, buffer sizes, partitioned/parallel reads, and connection pooling to sustain training throughput. - **FR-7 (Schema handling):** The framework shall detect or accept user-specified schemas and deterministically map source records to Python/NumPy/Tensor representations, with explicit handling of nulls and type mismatches. - **FR-8 (Credentials):** Authentication (database DSNs, AWS keys/IAM roles, Kerberos) shall be supplied via parameters, environment variables, or standard credential files; secrets must never be hardcoded. - **FR-9 (Error handling):** Connection failures, authorization errors, missing tables/objects, and malformed data shall raise informative, typed exceptions; transient faults shall be retried according to a configurable retry/backoff policy. - **FR-10 (Optional dependencies):** Backend-specific drivers (e.g., PyHive, boto3, pymysql) shall be optional extras; the framework core shall be importable without any backend driver installed.  ### Non-Functional Requirements  - **NFR-1 (Compatibility):** The framework shall operate on actively supported Python and PyTorch versions without modifying PyTorch core. - **NFR-2 (Performance):** Read throughput shall be comparable to direct native clients for each backend, with I/O overlapped against compute via prefetch and workers. - **NFR-3 (Usability):** Creating a DataLoader-ready dataset from any supported backend shall require minimal boilerplate and consistent, uniform APIs, with documented examples per backend. - **NFR-4 (Testability):** Each backend adapter shall be testable in CI using mocks/emulators (e.g., embedded databases, S3 simulators).  ### Acceptance Criteria  1. A user can construct a working `DataLoader` from a Hive table, a MySQL query, and an S3 prefix in fewer than 10 lines of code each. 2. A dataset exceeding available memory can be iterated for multiple epochs without OOM using the same user-facing API as in-memory datasets. 3. A third-party backend can be implemented and registered via the plugin interface without changes to library internals. 4. Switching between backends requires changing only connection/configuration parameters, not application code consuming the dataset.

issue_title: Add array unpacking/destructuring to GDScript
requirement: **Requirement: Array Unpacking (Destructuring) in GDScript**  GDScript shall support unpacking the elements of an array into multiple variables in a single statement.  1. **Declaration form:** A `var` declaration with a bracketed list of identifiers on the left-hand side and an array expression on the right-hand side shall assign each identifier the element at the corresponding index. Example: `var [x, y] = [1, 2]` results in `x == 1` and `y == 2`. 2. **Assignment form:** The same bracketed pattern shall be valid on the left-hand side of an assignment to existing variables, without the `var` keyword. Example: `[a, b] = [b, a]` swaps the values of `a` and `b`. 3. **Element count mismatch:** If the array has fewer elements than the pattern lists, the excess variables shall be set to `null` and a warning shall be emitted. If the array has more elements than the pattern lists, the extra elements shall be ignored, and a warning shall be emitted. 4. **Ignored elements:** The identifier `_` in a pattern shall skip the corresponding element without binding it to a variable. 5. **Non-array right-hand side:** If the right-hand side does not evaluate to an array, a runtime error shall be raised with a message identifying the type mismatch. 6. **Static analysis:** The parser and analyzer shall report a compile-time error for malformed patterns, such as duplicate identifiers within one pattern or non-identifier targets, unless they are `_`. 7. **Compatibility:** Existing GDScript code that uses square brackets in other contexts, such as indexing and array literals, shall continue to parse and execute unchanged. 8. **Documentation:** The GDScript reference shall document the syntax, the mismatch behavior, and examples for both declaration and assignment forms.

requirement: **Requirement: Conversion of Iterators to Fixed-Size Arrays**  The system shall provide a mechanism to convert the elements produced by an iterator into a fixed-size array.  **Details:**  - The conversion shall consume the iterator and place its elements, in iteration order, into a fixed-size array. - The target array length shall be known at compile time, and the element type shall be inferred from or specified by the iterator's item type. - If the iterator yields fewer elements than the array's length, the operation shall fail with a clear, documented error or return an indication of failure (for example, `None` or `Err`), rather than producing partially initialized memory. - If the iterator yields more elements than the array's length, the operation shall fail in the same manner, or the extra elements shall be explicitly handled according to documented behavior. - The operation shall not require heap allocation beyond what is needed for the array itself. - The mechanism shall be exposed as part of the public iterator or array API and documented with usage examples.

issue_title: net/http: support HTTP/3
requirement: **REQ: HTTP/3 Support in net/http**  **Requirement statement:** The `net/http` package shall support the HTTP/3 protocol (RFC 9114) for both client and server roles, enabling HTTP requests and responses to be exchanged over the QUIC transport (RFC 9000) using the existing `http.Request`, `http.ResponseWriter`, `http.Handler`, and `http.Client` interfaces without modification to user code.  **Sub-requirements:**  1. **Client support:** The package shall provide an HTTP/3-capable transport, configurable on `http.Client`, which uses HTTP/3 when the origin advertises it (e.g., via `Alt-Svc`) and transparently falls back to HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 over TCP when HTTP/3 is unavailable or the handshake fails. 2. **Server support:** The package shall provide an HTTP/3-capable server (or server configuration option) that serves HTTP/3 over QUIC while preserving existing `Handler`, middleware, and `ServeMux` semantics, and shall advertise HTTP/3 availability to clients via `Alt-Svc`. 3. **Protocol conformance:** Message semantics shall conform to RFC 9114 and RFC 9110, including QPACK header compression (RFC 9204), request/response body streaming, trailers, and error handling. 4. **Security:** All HTTP/3 connections shall use TLS 1.3 integrated with QUIC per RFC 9001; existing `tls.Config` options shall apply where meaningful. 5. **Configuration:** Users shall be able to enable, disable, and tune HTTP/3 behavior (e.g., 0-RTT, concurrent stream limits, flow-control windows, idle timeouts) via documented configuration fields, with HTTP/3 disabled by default.  **Constraints:**  - Existing public `net/http` APIs shall remain backward compatible; HTTP/3 shall be strictly opt-in. - Any QUIC implementation used shall comply with Go standard library dependency policy (internal implementation or explicitly approved dependency path). - The implementation shall pass conformance and interoperability testing against major HTTP/3 implementations (e.g., Chrome, curl, nginx, quic-go).  **Acceptance criteria:**  1. A server with HTTP/3 enabled serves concurrent requests from an HTTP/3-capable client over QUIC, verified by automated integration tests. 2. A client with HTTP/3 enabled establishes an HTTP/3 connection when the origin advertises it and transparently falls back to HTTP/2/1.1 otherwise, with no user-visible API changes. 3. Requests and responses—including streaming bodies and trailers—behave identically under HTTP/3 as under HTTP/2 for existing code. 4. Disabling HTTP/3 restores behavior identical to the prior release.

issue_title: Need negative trait bound
requirement: **Requirement: Support Negative Trait Bounds**  The compiler shall support negative trait bounds, written `!Trait`, in generic parameter bounds and `where` clauses. A negative bound asserts that a type parameter does not implement the named trait.  1. **Syntax:** Negative bounds shall be accepted in generic parameter lists (e.g., `fn f<T: !Copy>()`), `where` clauses (e.g., `where T: !Clone`), and `impl` headers (e.g., `impl<T: !Display> Trait for T`).  2. **Semantics:** A negative bound `T: !Trait` shall hold if and only if the trait solver can prove that `T: Trait` does not hold for the concrete type substituted for `T`. Trait selection shall treat a negative bound as satisfied only when no applicable implementation of `Trait` exists for that type.  3. **Coherence:** Impl coherence checking shall accept non-overlapping impls that are distinguished by negative bounds, such as a blanket impl for `T: !Trait` alongside an impl for `T: Trait`, without reporting conflicting implementations.  4. **Soundness across crates:** Negative reasoning shall be restricted so that adding an implementation of `Trait` in a downstream or upstream crate cannot silently change the meaning of a previously valid negative bound. Where this cannot be guaranteed, the compiler shall reject the bound or require the trait to be local or marked accordingly.  5. **Auto and marker traits:** Negative bounds shall be usable with auto traits (e.g., `T: !Send`) and marker traits, with behavior consistent with existing negative auto-trait impls.  6. **Associated types and projections:** Negative bounds shall apply to associated type projections (e.g., `T::Item: !Copy`) and shall be checked after projection normalization.  7. **Diagnostics:** When a negative bound is violated, the compiler shall emit an error that names the type, the trait, and the location of the bound, and shall point to the implementation that causes the violation if one exists.  8. **Compatibility:** Existing programs that do not use `!Trait` syntax shall compile with unchanged behavior and no new warnings. The feature shall be gated behind a feature flag until stabilization.  9. **Testing:** The test suite shall include positive and negative cases for each syntactic position, coherence with overlapping blanket impls, cross-crate scenarios, auto traits, and projection bounds.

issue_title: Implement method overloading in GDScript
requirement: **REQ-GDSCRIPT-042: Method Overloading Support**  GDScript shall support method overloading, enabling the declaration of multiple methods with the same identifier within a class, differentiated by parameter count, parameter types, or both. The compiler shall perform static overload resolution at call sites to select the most specific applicable method based on argument static types. Overloaded methods must be supported for instance methods, static methods (`static func`), and virtual methods, with full inheritance semantics allowing subclasses to override specific overloads or extend the overload set. Ambiguous calls where multiple overloads match equally well, or no overload matches the provided arguments, shall produce compile-time errors listing all candidate signatures. The feature must maintain full backward compatibility with existing GDScript code and integrate with the static type system, documentation generation, and IDE tooling (autocomplete and go-to-definition).  **Acceptance Criteria:** - Multiple `func` declarations with identical names but distinct signatures (e.g., `func process(value: int)` and `func process(value: String)`) compile successfully within the same class scope. - Method calls resolve to the correct overload at compile time based on static argument types without runtime overhead for statically typed calls. - Calls with arguments that match no overload, or match multiple overloads ambiguously (e.g., calling `foo(3.14)` when only `int` and `String` overloads exist), result in descriptive compile-time errors. - Overloading is supported in static methods, constructors (`_init`), and respects inheritance hierarchies including overriding individual overloads. - Existing GDScript projects compile and execute without modification or behavioral changes.

issue_title: Add support for splitting linker invocation to a second execution of `rustc`
requirement: **Requirement ID:** REQ-LINK-SPLIT-001  **Title:** Support splitting the linker invocation into a second execution of `rustc`  **Description:** The Rust compiler (`rustc`) shall support a two-phase build mode in which the linker invocation is decoupled from the compilation/codegen phase, allowing the link step to be performed by a second, separate execution of `rustc` rather than within the same invocation that performs compilation.  **Functional Requirements:**  1. **Link-deferred compilation mode:** `rustc` shall provide a command-line mechanism (e.g., a flag or option) that, when enabled, causes the compiler to perform compilation and codegen to completion but defer the linker invocation, emitting instead all artifacts and metadata required to perform linking at a later time.  2. **Link-only execution mode:** `rustc` shall provide a corresponding command-line mechanism that, when invoked in a subsequent execution, consumes the artifacts and link metadata produced by the deferred-compilation run and performs the actual linker invocation to produce the final output artifact (executable or dynamic library).  3. **Output equivalence:** The final artifact produced by the two-execution process (compile-then-link) shall be functionally equivalent to the artifact produced by a conventional single `rustc` invocation that compiles and links in one step, given identical inputs and compiler settings.  4. **Artifact completeness:** All information necessary for the second execution to link — including object files, library search paths, linker arguments, target-specific link options, and any codegen-produced inputs — shall be fully captured during the first execution such that the second execution does not need to recompile.  5. **Error handling and exit status:** The second execution shall correctly surface linker errors, warnings, and diagnostics to the user, and shall return an appropriate non-zero exit code if linking fails.  6. **Incremental compatibility:** The deferred link metadata shall be compatible with incremental compilation, such that a re-link following an unchanged compilation can be performed without redoing codegen.  7. **Backward compatibility:** Absent the new mechanism, `rustc` behavior shall remain unchanged: compilation and linking continue to occur within a single invocation by default.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - A crate can be built via two sequential `rustc` invocations (deferred-compile, then link-only) producing the same runnable artifact as a single combined invocation. - Linker failures in the second invocation are reported with correct diagnostics and exit codes. - Existing single-invocation builds show no behavioral change when the new flags are not used. - Cargo (or another build orchestrator) can drive the two-step process end to end without manual intervention.

issue_title: Using std::io::{Read, Write, Cursor} in a nostd environment
requirement: **Requirement: Provide `Read`, `Write`, and `Cursor` in `no_std` builds**  The library must be usable in `no_std` environments while still offering the familiar byte-stream abstractions from `std::io`. Specifically, the crate shall expose equivalents of `std::io::Read`, `std::io::Write`, and `std::io::Cursor` to downstream users in `no_std` builds (i.e. when the `std` feature is disabled), so that code operating on byte slices/buffers can read from and write to in-memory sources without depending on the standard library.  Requirements:  1. When compiled with `default-features = false` (no `std`), the crate shall provide public `Read` and `Write` traits with the same shape and semantics as `std::io::Read` / `std::io::Write` (notably `read`, `read_exact`, `read_to_end`, `write`, `write_all`, `flush`, and `write_fmt`-style behavior), including the associated `Error` type. 2. When compiled with `default-features = false`, the crate shall provide a `Cursor`-like type over an in-memory buffer (e.g. `Cursor<&[u8]>` / `Cursor<Vec<u8>>`) implementing `Read` and `Write`, with the same positional semantics (current position, `position()`, `set_position()`, `seek`-style behavior where applicable) as `std::io::Cursor`. 3. Implementations shall not require `std`; they must compile for `no_std` targets such as `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` and shall depend only on `core` (and `alloc` if dynamic buffers are needed). 4. The no_std implementations must be behaviorally compatible with their `std::io` counterparts: identical results for partial reads, `read_exact` erroring on unexpected EOF, `write_all` looping until all bytes are written, and cursor positions advancing exactly by the number of bytes transferred. 5. When the `std` feature *is* enabled, the crate's API must remain source-compatible with the previous behavior, and the `std::io` types must remain usable (either directly or via re-export/aliasing) so existing user code does not break. 6. The crate shall clearly document how to obtain these types in `no_std` builds, including any required feature flags, and the crate's CI/feature matrix shall verify that the no_std configuration compiles and its tests pass.
